articles.title: Microsoft responds to White House immigration crackdown as Trump honors Nadella
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: The Trump administration suspended Microsoft from the federal program the company uses to help foreign workers stay in the U.S. permanently, accusing the tech giant of abusing the system.

The announcement by Vice President JD Vance, during a news conference Thursday morning at the White House, came hours before President Trump gave Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation in a ceremony honoring Elon Musk and other tech leaders.

Vance said Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers last year while getting 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards, which he said amounted to replacing U.S. employees with lower-paid foreign workers.

“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft,” Vance said at the news conference, while adding, “Our message to Microsoft is you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers.”

Microsoft’s response: In a statement , the company said 80% of the roughly 6,000 H-1B applications it filed last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of people who already work for the company. The rest were for new hires who were already living in the U.S. legally, a group equal to about 1% of its U.S. workforce.
“They are not new arrivals to our country,” the company said.

Microsoft said it pays H-1B employees “the same as any other employees doing comparable work,” that its wages are “among the highest of all H-1B filings,” and that the vast majority of its U.S. employees are Americans.
The statement didn’t mention the suspension, but the company said it looks forward to “providing the Administration with additional information.”

Details of the penalty: The suspension covers the Labor Department’s Permanent Labor Certification program , known as PERM. It’s usually the first step when a company sponsors a foreign employee to live and work in the U.S. permanently. To get approved, the employer has to advertise the job and show the government that no qualified American worker was available.

Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the department won’t accept new applications from Microsoft or process the ones it already has pending. The move doesn’t stop Microsoft from applying for H-1B visas, the temporary work visas that many PERM applicants hold.
The department also suspended Adobe and six IT outsourcing firms: Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.

Trump didn’t mention the suspension at the ceremony. Introducing Nadella, he credited him with making Microsoft “an early leader in superintelligence” and said, “Satya, we are honored to give you the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. It is so well deserved.”

The official citation honored Nadella “for his transformative leadership of a critical American technology company” and for building the “hyperscale infrastructure that enabled the training and global deployment of American superintelligence.”
Tech industry reaction: The announcement drew pushback in Seattle’s tech community.

“There has been a continuous, nonstop deluge of immigration-related news leading up to the midterms,” said Xiao Wang , co-founder and CEO of Boundless , a Seattle startup that helps people navigate the U.S. immigration process.

Wang pushed back on Vance’s characterization of H-1B workers as “foreign indentured servants,” noting there are wage requirements to prevent underpayment of employees. He emphasized the economic benefits of educating and employing the students and workers who seek these visas — and what happens if they’re discouraged or prevented from coming to the U.S.
“What I have been trying to warn folks about is the long-term chilling effects that would be detrimental to the long-term prosperity and competitiveness of the United States,” he said.

Wang said the idea that the layoffs and recruitment of foreign-born workers are linked doesn’t make sense. “Layoffs and hiring are not one for ones of each other, especially at giant companies like Microsoft,” he said.
Someone laid off from a gaming division at Microsoft isn’t interchangeable, for example, with an H-1B employee who’s an expert in agentic AI for a Copilot role, he said.

Priyanka Kulkarni , founder and CEO of the immigration technology company Casium , previously worked at Microsoft for more than a decade building enterprise AI technology. She personally navigated H-1B status before becoming a permanent resident.

“I worked alongside people from around the world whose expertise helped build technology used by American businesses every day,” she said, adding, “America wants to lead in AI. That requires attracting and retaining exceptional people, and giving them confidence that they can build a future here.”
Kulkarni called the phrase “foreign indentured servants” troubling, and said it exposes a contradiction in the administration’s action.

“If the concern is that workers depend too heavily on their employers, blocking their path to permanent residency could deepen that dependence,” she said. “Permanent residency gives people more freedom to change jobs, negotiate pay, and start businesses.”

articles.title: Rocket fuel: Seattle-area startups raise a record $3.5B as national VC funding cools
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Seattle-area startups raised $3.5 billion in venture capital in the third quarter, the most in any quarter going back at least a decade, led by big rounds for Kent-based rocket maker Stoke Space , Bellevue developer platform Temporal and Everett fusion company Helion .

That’s more than triple the $1 billion raised in the region in the same quarter a year earlier, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor . It’s also more than $1 billion above the previous quarterly high of about $2.4 billion, reached in late 2018 and again in late 2022.

Most of the money went to a handful of companies building physical things: rockets, satellites, spacecraft and fusion power plants. Three space companies in the region raised $1.6 billion combined: Stoke, Redmond-based Starcloud and Seattle’s Hubble Network .

Nationally, the trend went the other way. U.S. venture funding fell 40% from the prior quarter, to $98.4 billion, as the giant rounds for frontier AI labs that drove the first half of the year tapered off.

Seattle ranked seventh among U.S. metro areas for venture dollars in the quarter. The Bay Area led with $40.7 billion, followed by Los Angeles, New York, Austin, Boston and Denver. Denver’s $4.2 billion came largely from a single $3.9 billion round for AI data center developer Crusoe.
By number of deals, Seattle ranked eighth, with 94.

The total includes Helion’s $500 million round, which the company announced in June but PitchBook counts in the third quarter. Even without it, the quarter would still be the region’s biggest on record.

articles.title: UW protein institute run by Nobel winner lands giant AI cloud grant from Nvidia CEO’s foundation
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: The UW Medicine Institute for Protein Design (IPD) has announced a giant grant of computing power from the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation, supercharging its research into new protein discovery.

“We have made more rapid progress on methods development than any time in my career,” said David Baker, director of the IPD and a 2024 Nobel laureate in chemistry. “I mean, it’s just been totally mind-boggling.”

In June, the IPD began accessing Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, through the cloud computing company CoreWeave. The grant from the foundation, which was co-founded by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, totals nearly 7 million GPU hours. The allocation is expected to support the institute for a year.

The IPD’s work has long been rooted in computation. In 2003, Baker and fellow University of Washington researchers used their Rosetta software to design a protein with a structure unlike any known in nature. In recent years, the institute has embraced deep learning, releasing tools such as RoseTTAFold for predicting protein structures and RFdiffusion for designing new proteins.

With this technology, the institute designs previously unimagined proteins with potential for treating intractable diseases and tackling environmental challenges such as plastic waste and toxic pollutants. The tools are open source and available for public use.

Running them takes vast computing power, though, and until now the institute has lacked the resources to pay for outside cloud services. It has relied instead on its own computer cluster, which works but is limited. Baker said IPD scientists meet every Tuesday at 5 p.m. to decide what to test over the coming week, keeping capacity in mind.

To advance their protein research, the team experiments with different architectures for the AI models and tweaks the datasets used for training, sometimes expanding them or adding synthetic data. With compute restrictions, however, researchers historically have made multiple changes at once rather than testing each alteration individually, a more systematic approach that yields cleaner results.
Despite the hurdles, the IPD has produced a steady stream of breakthroughs with its models and protein designs, publishing regularly in leading scientific journals such as Nature and Science.

Google DeepMind is pursuing similar AI-driven protein research. Baker said he knew the tech giant’s team had much more computing power than the IPD, but he didn’t fully appreciate what that could unlock.
That capacity “spawns more ideas because you know you can test them,” Baker said. “So it just creates this incredibly fertile, creative environment.”

Jensen Huang, the foundation’s co-president, said in a statement that the extra computing power allows the UW researchers to train AI “on tens of millions of molecular structures, learning from virtual experiments, and finding novel protein designs that have eluded nature.”
Huang predicted that many of the most important future medicines “will come from proteins that have never existed.”
Baker said the IPD still holds its Tuesday meetings, but the new compute capabilities — which he called “transformational” — open up more options.
“The team is iterating fast,” Baker said. “We get feedback on all these different computational architecture explorations, and there’s just so many different things you can try.”

articles.title: Fast-growing AI startup Nscale doubles Bellevue office footprint to 46K square feet
articles.author: John Cook
paras: AI infrastructure startup Nscale is doubling down on its new Seattle-area presence before even opening the doors.

After initially leasing a single floor at The Eight tower in downtown Bellevue earlier this year, the London-based company has expanded by an additional floor, bringing its total footprint in the new development to approximately 46,000 rentable square feet, according to a report from The Broderick Group.

The expansion signals an aggressive ramp-up for Nscale’s primary U.S. engineering hub, slated to open in January 2027. While the initial 24,000-square-foot lease was pegged to accommodate up to 250 employees, the added space gives the fast-growing cloud provider room to scale its local team even further beyond its current 50 Seattle-area workers.
Founded in 2024, Nscale is riding a massive wave of capital and growth.
It raised a $2 billion Series C round at a $14.6 billion valuation earlier this year, backed by Nvidia, Dell, Citadel, Jane Street, and Point72, alongside a $900 million credit line.

The company also earlier this year hired Nidhi Chappell, the former Microsoft corporate vice president who led Azure AI and high-performance computing infrastructure, including the supercomputers that power ChatGPT. As Nscale’s new president of AI infrastructure, based in the Seattle area, Chappell will oversee the company’s global engineering and data center operations.

“I’ve had a front-row seat to some of the biggest moments in AI over the past several years, but one thing has always stood out: the world remembers the breakthroughs, but it’s the people building the infrastructure behind the scenes who make them possible,” Chappell wrote in a LinkedIn post earlier this year announcing the company’s first “onboarding” event in Seattle.
Nscale’s new office is set to open in January, with the second floor slated to open in June, reports The Puget Sound Business Journal .

The company’s growth underscores Bellevue’s growing magnetism for out-of-town AI players. The company joins a dense ecosystem of AI infrastructure and application hubs establishing outposts on the Eastside, including xAI, OpenAI, Databricks, CoreWeave, Armada, and Anduril.

articles.title: Overland AI unveils IBEX, a new autonomous ground vehicle selected by the Marine Corps
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Seattle defense startup Overland AI has unveiled IBEX , a new fully autonomous ground vehicle selected by the U.S. Marine Corps to support counter-drone air defense operations and execute high-risk frontline missions, including resupply, breaching, and electronic warfare.

IBEX was developed under a Department of War APFIT production contract that recently expanded to $25 million with added funding for the Army’s 75th Ranger Regiment. The initial $20 million milestone deal made Overland AI the first ground autonomy startup to serve as a primary defense hardware supplier, with the Marine Corps selecting the platform for integration into its Marine Air Defense Integrated System (MADIS).

Built on the chassis, engine, and drivetrain of the Polaris MRZR — an ultra-light utility vehicle already used, fueled, and maintained across the armed forces — IBEX can carry a 2,000-pound payload and reach fully autonomous speeds exceeding 35 mph. The vehicle offers a 250-mile cruising range at 20 mph and is sized to fit inside a V-22 Osprey for air transport.

IBEX is powered by Overland AI’s proprietary OverDrive software stack, which combines real-time terrain perception with adaptive route planning to navigate complex, off-road environments at speed without relying on GPS signals or pre-mapped routes. Drivers can control multiple uncrewed vehicles simultaneously using OverWatch, the startup’s command-and-control software.

IBEX provides 5 kW of export power to run onboard sensors and defense systems, addressing energy limits in forward field operations. The company describes each vehicle as a combined power, communications, and compute node designed to operate independently in environments with limited or disrupted communications.

“We pride ourselves on developing technology that is informed directly by the warfighter,” Greg Okopal, co-founder and chief operating officer of Overland AI, said in a statement, adding that IBEX can be deployed on day one and maintained with the parts and fuel units already have.

The vehicle joins the startup’s existing flagship platform, ULTRA, as the company continues scaling production at its Seattle manufacturing facility to meet growing military demand for autonomous ground systems.
Founded in 2022 as a spinout from the University of Washington, Overland AI has rapidly expanded its defense operations, raising $100 million in Series B funding earlier this year.
The startup — No. 7 on the GeekWire 200 ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups — has raised over $140 million in venture funding to date.

In 2025, Overland opened a 22,000-square-foot production facility in the Rainier Beach neighborhood south of downtown Seattle. And this summer, the startup established an engineering outpost in Burlingame, Calif., aiming to tap into the Bay Area’s robotics and autonomy talent pool.
Overland AI’s growth reflects a broader defense technology boom across the Seattle region, where established firms and fast-growing startups are building major hardware and software footprints.

Companies expanding in the region include Shield AI , which selected the Seattle area for a massive manufacturing facility to build its autonomous X-BAT fighter jet; Anduril , which sees a path to 1,000 Seattle-area engineers across its Bellevue and Seattle hubs; and Echodyne , which opened a $40 million radar manufacturing factory in Woodinville to support drone detection demand.

articles.title: Shield AI lands $150M Navy contract to advance AI-piloted fighter jet that will be built south of Seattle
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Defense technology startup Shield AI has secured a $150 million contract from the U.S. Navy to advance development of its X-BAT autonomous fighter jet — providing fresh federal backing for the program as the company establishes its first major manufacturing footprint south of Seattle.

Last week, GeekWire reported on Shield AI’s plans to open a 420,000-square-foot engineering and production facility in Des Moines, Wash., dubbed “X-Forge 3.” The company, which is looking to add an additional one million square feet of space in the region, said it expects to employ about 4,000 workers in the Seattle area by the early 2030s.

The new $150 million contract with the Navy adds funding from the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment through its Defense Exportability Features program. The agreement supports efforts to design security and export capabilities directly into the X-BAT, a process that enables advanced U.S. military hardware to eventually be sold to international allies without exposing sensitive domestic technologies.
San Diego-based Shield AI, which raised a $2 billion venture capital round at a $12.7 billion valuation earlier this year, is matching the award with $150 million of its own capital.

Combined with a prior $100 million joint investment finalized in August under the Navy and Defense Innovation Unit’s (DIU) expeditionary strike effort, cumulative commitments behind the X-BAT now stand at $400 million.

Designed to take off and land vertically, the X-BAT is built to operate from amphibious assault ships, destroyers, commercial cargo decks, and highway strips without relying on traditional concrete runways or aircraft carrier catapults. It launches from a specialized Launch and Recovery Vehicle — a mobile trailer that erects the jet vertically, allowing it to be towed on interstate highways or loaded onto ships.

At the time of its introduction last year, Shield AI co-founder and president Brandon Tseng, a former Navy SEAL, called X-BAT a “transformative, runway-independent aircraft” and noted that “airpower without runways is the holy grail of deterrence.”

The urgency behind runway-independent airpower was underscored last weekend when the U.S. Air Force withdrew strategic B-1 bombers from R.A.F. Fairford in Britain following reports of potential drone threats targeting the air base.

Shield AI expects to begin producing aircraft in Des Moines in 2028, scaling to a target production rate of roughly 150 jets per year by the early 2030s. While prototyping is based in Frisco, Texas, and flight testing will take place at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas, the Des Moines plant will house the core production line and engineering teams.
In an interview with GeekWire, Shield AI executives emphasized the speed at which it hopes to roll out the AI-piloted aircraft in Des Moines.

“This is a large program,” Armor Harris , senior vice president of aircraft at Shield AI, told GeekWire. “Building a next generation fighter jet is no small endeavor, and with the amount of interest that we’ve seen, both from our U.S. government customers and from international customers, we could be looking at building these at rates greater than fighter jets have been built in a really long time.”
Harris noted that keeping development and manufacturing closely linked allows the company to move significantly faster than traditional defense procurement cycles.

“We are testing early and often while working on the aircraft, mission systems, ship suitability and production in parallel,” Harris said in Thursday’s press release. “That approach helps us identify and resolve issues earlier, reduce development risk and move more quickly toward flight testing.”
An engineering team of roughly 500 across Shield AI and key suppliers — including GE Aerospace — is currently building flight-test aircraft.

While the X-BAT has yet to make its maiden flight, the program cleared major hardware milestones in mid-2026. Engineers completed ground engine light-off and thrust-vectoring nozzle integration using GE Aerospace’s F110 engine, alongside wind-tunnel testing to validate internal weapons bay aerodynamics at both low and high speeds.

The aircraft is powered by Shield AI’s Hivemind autonomy software, an AI pilot designed to execute tactical strike missions in contested environments where GPS and satellite communications are jammed.
The jet features a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius and a 2,000-nautical-mile total range, topping the estimated 590-nautical-mile combat radius of the conventional Lockheed Martin F-35A.
Initial flight tests are scheduled for late 2026 in Kansas, with first production aircraft deliveries targeted for late 2028.

“X-BAT is being built to enhance the lethality, survivability and combat power of U.S. Naval Aviation,” said J.J. “Yank” Cummings, Shield AI’s head of mission solutions for the U.S. Navy and former commanding officer of the aircraft carrier USS Gerald R. Ford. “Its runway-independent design and small deck footprint can increase sortie generation and extend long-range air combat power.”

articles.title: Pollet and Dreher Hone Their Pitch to Urbanists in LD46 Race
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Depending how the November election goes, the residents of the 46th Legislative District in Northwest Seattle could have a new state representative after Rep. Gerry Pollet drew a relatively strong challenge from former federal prosecutor Will Dreher. Dreher has staked his campaign on a bid to lead the charge for artificial intelligence regulations, while Pollet is leaning on his experience, and his campaign has pitched him as the real progressive in the race.
In a three-way race, Pollet finished the primary on top, with 51.6% of the primary vote. Dreher won nearly 31% and has serious ground to close if he hopes to pull off the upset.

Plus, the dynamic of the race got a little weird after the primary. Tech entrepreneur and progressive rabblerouser Ron Davis, who The Urbanist Election Committee (on which I serve) endorsed , was eliminated after pulling in 16% of the vote. Rather than endorsing the other challenger or simply riding off into the sunset, Davis enthusiastically endorsed Pollet , and took to sharply attacking Dreher and defending Pollet via two long posts on his website, Rondevous .

Also catching criticism from Davis was The Stranger , which endorsed Dreher in the primary. "Let’s unleash this blue-blooded Yankee on the billionaire tech lobby that writes our laws in Olympia," The Stranger wrote. That endorsement likely sealed Davis' loss, although the gulf between the candidates was large enough he may have lost anyway.

"I came back to the same inexorable conclusion I reached in early July: that The Stranger's endorsements really are that powerful, and that it's nearly impossible for a progressive to overcome its influence even with a strong campaign and a lot of grassroots support," Davis wrote in August.

After his primary loss, Davis alleged Pollet – despite his earlier decision to challenge him for his seat – wasn't so bad, and was actually a standout on a number of issues, including education and progressive taxation.

The move came as a surprise to some urbanists who tracked Pollet's anti-urbanist positions early in his career, such as opposing bike lanes in Wedgwood and obstructing statewide housing reform. In contrast, Dreher is a regular cyclist and has pledged to be a reliable pro-housing vote.

"I bike commuted for about four or five years after the pandemic started downtown from my house in Ravenna, and you know one of the things that I very quickly learned as a bike commuter was, I mean, for me personally at least, that I was not comfortable biking with traffic," Dreher told The Urbanist . "And that the number one thing for both safety and to increase the actual uptake of biking seems to have obviously not just protected bike lanes, but protected bike trails and making sure that we have a robust connected trail network."

Dreher said the state should invest more in transit and pursue congestion pricing to make roads work better for all, following in the footsteps of New York City's new highly successful congestion pricing system in Lower Manhattan.

"Manhattan is a very small island in the grand scheme of things relative to the population of New York City," Dreher said. "Downtown Seattle is a land constrained area, with only so many ways to get in or out, and congestion pricing - it's true - is useful for and can be used for raising revenue, but you know I view its primary purpose as modifying behavior in a way that helps the fight against climate change, right? And in a way that helps make our downtown both less congested, have less local pollution, and in general be helping to encourage folks to use alternative ways to get downtown."
While he granted it would take time, Dreher expressed interest in being part of a coalition advancing congestion pricing.

"The good thing is that we now have some cities that are actually exploring, and not just exploring in theory, but actually in practice using congestion pricing, and the sky has not fallen," Dreher said. "My hope would be that we can start to build a coalition around what I think is a fairly sensible policy solution that more cities in the United States should be using. [...] It's something that I think makes a ton of sense. It's something that I think we just need to start having that conversation now in order to make it become a reality at some point in the near future."

On housing issues, Dreher told The Urbanist he is interested in pursuing a statewide funded inclusionary zoning program and in exploring a land value tax. He also pledged to be a reliable vote on housing abundance, although his campaign website did formerly use some "neighborhood character"-type language that Davis portrayed as dog whistles for "not in my backyard" (NIMBY) housing opponents. Dreher has since removed the language and told The Urbanist that it was an honest mistake, rather than a dog whistle.

Dreher's linguistic choices aside, Pollet was such an obstacle as chair of the House Local Government Committee that I named him to the "zeroes" list in our annual legislative recap after the 2021 and 2022 sessions.
Davis himself noted the cost of delays from housing reform holdouts like Pollet when in his campaign rollout interview with The Urbanist back in March.

“Those years were low-interest-rate years. We could have tens of thousands, maybe 50,000 or 100,000 more modestly-priced homes in the region right now, and they would be bidding over us, instead of us bidding over what’s left. And that’s a really huge and ugly, frustrating dynamic,” Davis told The Urbanist at the time.

That frustration seemed to extend to members of the Democratic caucus, who removed Pollet as chair following the 2022 session. Democrats came back in 2023 and finally succeeded in passing statewide middle housing reform via House Bill 1110. That law recently bore fruit as the mandate kicked in last year in many cities, including Seattle , which finally phased out restrictive single family zoning and allowed fourplexes or greater citywide after more than a decade of flirting with the idea to no avail.

Pollet ended up voting for HB 1110, but not before pressing his colleagues to pass an amendment allowing up to a quarter of an affected city's residential land to be carved out of rezones by citing displacement risk. In practice, the logistics of the displacement-risk carveouts have proven complicated enough that most cities have avoided them.

Fast forward to 2026 and Pollet has the endorsement of some of the legislature's most well-known urbanists, like Rep. Julia Reed (D-36th LD, Queen Anne), and Nicole Macri and Shaun Scott (D-43rd LD, Capitol Hill).

"I know I've evolved," Pollet told The Urbanist during an interview last month. "It's important to evolve and learn and realize that I wasn't as steeped in it as I needed to be on some aspects of middle housing, I was much more focused on housing issues relating to multifamily and transit-oriented development than middle housing."

Pollet portrayed himself as better at spotting when local activists were simply making excuses, rather than raising genuine concerns, such as the frequent excuse that neighborhoods need more robust infrastructure before they can accept housing growth, whether beefier roads or utilities or bigger schools.

"One of the things I learned is that listening to people who said, 'Well, we don't have the infrastructure,' was a NIMBY response that we needed to say, 'We're going to force you to have the infrastructure if you truly don't.' But we're not just going to take your word for it because it's often a NIMBY response, and that's an example of where I feel I was very conscious of my changing position that we have to force local governments to do that."

In illustrating how he's evolved and become an asset for the urbanist coalition that rattled off a string of policy wins in recent legislative sessions, Pollet pointed out he helped ensure that statewide parking reform passed in 2025 .

"I not only voted for it, but when it came to the floor of the House, we were briefed on it in caucus, and it ran into a roadblock that nearly pulled it from the schedule," Pollet said, before launching into a story about he helped broker an agreement between his colleagues and disability rights advocates to ensure those concerns did not derail the parking reform bill.

Davis, who met with The Urbanist along with Pollet last month shortly after endorsing him, vouched for his former rival, saying he was a big help in passing parking reform, which Davis was lobbying for on behalf of the Sightline Institute. (Of course, not so helpful overall that he opted against challenging him for his seat.)

Given his background, Pollet is naturally sympathetic to environmental concerns and is skeptical of efforts to streamline the State Environmental Policy Act, which has been criticized as a needless hurdle for housing projects, often hijacked by degrowth activists and NIMBYs to delay projects. Pollet's roots and his road to politics are in environmental law.

"I went to law school at the UW to be an environmental public interest attorney," Pollet told The Urbanist during a September interview. "[I] led the effort to stop Hanford from being a high-level nuclear waste dump, working with the Yakima [Tribe] to protect Gable Mountain, which is sacred to them, and ran the statewide ballot initiative to stop that in 1986, and then founded the organization leading work on the cleanup of Hanford, and along the way, you know, I was very active on many of our groundbreaking environmental laws in the state, including helping draft the Growth Management Act. I was one of the five or six authors of our state Superfund law model, and lobbied on many many environmental laws and helped pass many of them in our state."
Dreher, like Davis, is a Harvard Law trained attorney. Dreher followed in the footsteps of his father, who was a top environmental lawyer for the Clinton and Obama administrations.

Dreher famously clerked for Brett Kavanaugh , the Trump-nominated judge who won a lifetime appointment on the U.S. Supreme Court in 2018. Dreher signed a letter of support for that bid, along with fellow former law clerks. Davis used that as a frequent attack line on the campaign trail, but it didn't seem to fully resonate with voters, given the primary result.

After Kavanaugh's Supreme Court nomination happened in 2018 and the sexual assault allegations against him came out, Dreher said he changed his mind and withdrew his support. Dreher later that year signed onto a second letter supporting an FBI investigation of the allegations.

In 2019, Dreher joined the Department of Justice under the Trump administration as an Assistant U.S. Attorney in the Western District of Washington. His website notes "Dreher has the rare distinction of having prosecuted 25 January 6th insurrectionists." He spent over five years as a federal prosecutor, before leaving to join private practice as a litigator at the firm Keller Rohrback.

Dreher helped lead the firm's artificial intelligence litigation group and was appointed Co-Lead Interim Class Counsel in the copyright infringement class action Hendrix et al. v. Apple, Inc . The case alleges copyright infringement over texts Apple fed into its large language model or LLM, without permission from the authors or publishers.
Dreher has made reining in AI platforms and the tech giants behind them as a centerpiece of his campaign.

"The primary impetus for me getting in this particular race now was really just how rapidly accelerating, I think, our challenges with artificial intelligence and technology more broadly," Dreher said. "So like data privacy, mass surveillance, social media use with kids. There were just a number of tech issues that I've been working on in my current job for the last couple of years, but that I just had seen very little progress on at the state legislature, and I think even beyond that, very little focus on those issues."

Dreher pointed out that the Trump administration seemed to be going in the opposite direction, embracing a rapid expansion of AI applications for short-term financial gain. The state, meanwhile, has been flatfooted when it comes to regulating AI, in his estimation.

"My daughter, who's nine, always talks about how she wants to be a teacher when she grows up," Dreher said. "And Melania Trump in March, came out and had a rollout with a robot teacher and said, 'This will be the future of education.' And I'd say that was really the moment where it fully clicked or crystallized – that I just felt like I needed to do something to try to make sure that that was not the future of education, and more broadly, to try to kickstart or jumpstart our state to start taking seriously that battle."

On the other hand, Dreher's critics – with Davis at the vanguard – have questioned whether Dreher is ready to take on the tech giants so heavily invested in infusing AI into American life. They've pointed out that employees at the AI firm Anthropic were a top source of donations for Dreher's campaign, much of that money from out of state. Pollet, himself, seemed to take offense that Dreher was seeking to claim ownership of education reform, AI, and data privacy regulation issues, which he saw the state legislature as already making significant headway on.

"My thought is same thing goes as education. How would he know? He's not lobbied one day on these issues in Olympia," Pollet told The Urbanist . "There are legislators who know a lot more than him about those issues, and like part of that is the data center issues, right? And you know, he started this campaign, and I don't think he knew that I and others, working with [Rep.] Beth Doglio, had introduced what is viewed nationally as a model bill in terms of regulating data centers. And on data privacy, I don't think he knows, for example, what the battle has been in this state, and we have really strong champions on data privacy."
While not as versed in urbanist bread-and-butter topics as Davis, Dreher still sees himself as the standard-bearer for those issues now that Davis has been knocked out of the race.

"I frankly appreciate Ron's expertise and experience on a number of the issues that we've talked about, housing and transit issues in particular," Dreher said. "I was happy that that was one of the focuses in the race, and I intend to continue to make it a focus for the rest of the race. But now... the voters maybe have a somewhat simplified decision to make between myself and Representative Pollet."

articles.title: Capitol Hill is getting a furry store as Furesh sets up shop on E Pike
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Furry folks celebrating Pride on Broadway last summer
The Furesh crew at work (Image: Furesh.Shop)
What will happen when a wolf and hyena open a shop in Seattle dedicated to furry artists and creators? E Pike will find out in 2027 when Furesh opens its new Capitol Hill store.

The costume design and fabrication studio has grown as a specialist in custom fursuit craftsmanship, with an emphasis on tailored bodysuits engineered for mobility, durability, and comfort, as well as standalone parts like paws and tails.

articles.title: What the Seattle Parks ‘Healthy Capitol Hill Hike’ fitness equipment for people and dogs looks like
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Seattle Parks and Recreation has officially debuted the Healthy Capitol Hill Hike , an outdoor fitness initiative allowing neighborhood residents and their dogs to work out together across Capitol Hill.
CHS reported here on the initiative touted earlier this year by the city as part of activation efforts to help address public safety issues in parks across Capitol Hill and the Central District.

Seattle Parks has not said what the total budget for the installations tallies up to but said it was planned to keep costs minimal and draw on existing resources. Infrastructure ranges from heavy duty parks-style human workout equipment seen in public spaces across the country to a row of poles now installed in the middle of Broadway Hill Park as a dog agility station.

The low-budget project adds human- and dog-friendly fitness equipment alongside bodyweight workout stations to eight neighborhood green spaces, including Broadway Hill , Tashkent Park, Seven Hills Park, Summit Slope Park, and Williams Place . Designed through local community feedback, the effort aims to boost park safety and neighborhood accessibility.

Starting at Cal Anderson Park , visitors can choose between a 1.6-mile loop featuring upper-body exercise recommendations or a 1.5-mile loop focused on lower-body movements. Walkers and runners can also link both paths together for a complete 5K course. Digital route maps and suggested workouts are available online from seattle.gov .

articles.title: 19 Capitol Hill and Central District organizations and businesses join call for Seattle to move $8M in budget from hiring more cops to spending more on artists
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: More than 600 artists and 116 organizations have delivered an open letter to Mayor Katie Wilson and the Seattle City Council urging amendments to the 2027 budget that would reallocate police hiring funds toward cultural infrastructure.

Amid a looming $175 million deficit, the mayor’s proposal slates a $68 million increase for the Seattle Police Department to recruit 66 officers. The coalition requests council members redirect $8 million from that proposed increase directly into the Office of Arts and Culture .

“By paying local artists to bring life to our streets, parks, and business districts, the city fostered deep community engagement,” the letter reads. “These activations increased positive foot traffic, built relationships among neighbors, and created a vibrant cultural presence everywhere from North of Downtown to the South End.”
Capitol Hill and Central District Organizations and Businesses

Signatories argue that placemaking serves as vital public safety infrastructure, pointing to a $3.6 million investment in 2025 that funded 120 grants and 80 public activations ahead of the World Cup summer.
The letter credits that initiative with curbing violence and yielding a “murder-free June.”
The requested $8 million would more than double the 2025 cultural investment to establish year-round community programming citywide.

CHS reported here on Wilson’s proposal which would wipe out a $175 million deficit without tax increases or withdrawals from city reserves. The proposal would cut roughly $50 million annually in General Fund spending by eliminating 128 positions and aligning departmental budgets with historical costs, pairing these cuts with $50 million in shuffled funding by leveraging JumpStart payroll tax revenues to cover core services and homelessness programs.
Starting next week, budget chair Dan Strauss will lead the process as council members are briefed on policy considerations before officially proposing potential amendments to the mayor’s proposal.

District 3 representative Council President Joy Hollingsworth has signaled her support for continued police and anti-crime investments, joining a call for the mayor to strengthen her public safety plan .
A final “all-day” public hearing is scheduled for November 5th .

articles.title: Sound Transit opens 2027 budget and levy review under reworked financial plan
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Sound Transit opened public review for its 2027 Budget and Property Tax Levy with a Thursday morning hearing as the agency begins implementing major financial adjustments to address soaring costs and stretched timelines.

The upcoming spending plan marks the first annual cycle governed by the board’s refreshed ST3 affordability framework, designed to tackle what was a projected $34.5 billion program shortfall extending through 2046.

Earlier this year, the board approved a major package of deferrals and cuts t o address the projected shortfall. The new financial outlook would have Sound Transit on track for expansion to West Seattle by 2032 and Ballard by 2042.

Meanwhile, light rail has now reached the Central District as Judkins Park Station celebrated its grand opening in March, part of a full transformation into a two-line system — the original 1 Line serving the city and its north-south neighbors, and now the added 2 Line connecting Seattle to Bellevue and Redmond on the world’s first light rail on a floating bridge.
There have also been smaller points of progress including the opening of a new in-fill station in Pinehurst .

Big changes are ahead for riders at busy Capitol Hill Station where Sound Transit has announced it will add fare gates as part of a 14 station pilot. The installations are planned to be complete in either 2029 or 2030 after the completion of a design and rollout plan for the $87 million pilot program.

For Sound Transit’s fiscal environment, key policy changes taking effect in 2027 include regionalizing debt interest costs across district subareas and restarting delivery on deferred capital items, including the $315 million Sounder Maintenance Base. Funds will also reflect route restructuring outlined in the draft 2027 Service Plan across King, Pierce, and Snohomish counties.
The agency’s property tax levy remains capped at $0.25 per $1,000 of assessed value under the voter approved ST3, with annual revenue growth on existing parcels limited to 1% by state law.
Final budget adoption and levy certification are scheduled for late 2026.

articles.title: Free Will Astrology
articles.author: Rob Brezsny
paras: ARIES (March 21-April 19): “Dear Oracle: My secret terror is being ordinary. I need to be special, and lately I’m worried I’m just average and unremarkable. That thought is repugnant to me! Can you offer any advice? —Afraid of Average.” Dear Afraid: The pressure to be extraordinary is exhausting because it’s the wrong goal. Your birthright and your life assignment aren’t about being special in the sense of better-than. You’re simply meant to be vividly, generously, amazingly yourself. In the coming weeks, I invite you to trade the anxious hunt for superiority for the warm, throbbing joy of full self-expression. Shine because it feels fantastic, not to outrank anyone.

TAURUS (April 20-May 20): Here’s a hypothesis worth entertaining: You don’t fully know everything you want. Not yet. Not at the core, where desire isn’t well-behaved but turns wild and intense. Your fluency with surface desire can sometimes keep you from excavating the mysteries that live below it. The familiar longings override the stranger, stronger ones that haven’t found their bearings. So there are aspects of your primal yearnings that remain unexamined, simply because they require a particular stillness and courage to unearth completely. The good news: Now is an unusually favorable time to go looking.

GEMINI (May 21-June 20): The Taurus philosopher Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life must be lived forward but can only be understood backward. You Geminis are naturally inclined to resist that advice. Many of you analyze experiences while they’re still unfolding. Can I coax you to try a different approach in the coming weeks? As usual, you may be tempted to figure everything out immediately. But the most useful clarity won’t arrive until later, as you survey what has occurred and recognize patterns you couldn’t see in real time. So try to stay curious rather than overly diagnostic. Keep gathering impressions, stories, and clues. Allow events to transpire like chapters in a book whose ending you haven’t reached yet.

CANCER (June 21-July 22): The Germans have a word, *Sehnsucht*, for a feeling that my English language can’t quite convey: a deep, sweet, aching longing for something you can’t name. It may be a faraway home you’ve never visited or a wholeness you seem to remember without ever having had it. Most people treat this yearning as a problem to be fixed or numbed. But I think it’s sacred information, Cancerian, and you’re especially fluent in it right now. Don’t rush to resolve the ache or explain it away. Instead, follow it like a scent. What is your Sehnsucht pointing toward? Let it lead you toward the beauty and meaning your soul is homesick for.

LEO (July 23-Aug. 22): Botanists know that climbing vines have a simple approach. They keep extending their sensitive tendrils until they discover something sturdy enough to support upward growth. Their progress depends on continual experimentation. I love it when you imitate this style of intelligence, Leo, which I think will be especially useful and successful during the coming weeks. So instead of demanding guarantees before beginning a new endeavor, offer exploratory feelers. Ask friendly questions. Test prototypes. The right support system probably already exists, but may not reveal itself until you reach toward it.

VIRGO (Aug. 23-Sept. 22): One of my favorite Virgos works in a museum cleaning centuries-old paintings with exquisite patience. She uses tiny swabs and gentle solvents to lift away layers of darkened varnish and grime. She’s an expert at making the original colors emerge so vividly that the painting looks newly made. But her work demands artful restraint. If she presses too hard or applies the wrong solvent, she could destroy the very thing she means to reveal. This approach can be your specialty in the coming weeks, Virgo. I hope you will attend to valuables that have been obscured by accumulated grime, like old habits, stale assumptions, and other people’s projections. Your task is to gently lift it all away and let the true colors shine.

LIBRA (Sept. 23-Oct. 22): Periodically, you have the cosmic right to receive precisely what you need. Life is duty-bound to deliver a close approximation of full satisfaction. I believe now is one of those times. So please be bold and articulate about naming the specific blessings you require. Write them down, speak them aloud, and pray for them—not as a demand, but as a hearty invitation. Then, for a while, live as if all of creation is indeed honor-bound to respond accordingly, adjusting its behavior so it’s in harmony with the gifts you’ve asked for.

SCORPIO (Oct. 23-Nov. 21): Every Thursday night, I haul my trash bin out to the street so the collectors can empty it the following morning. Most weeks it’s three-quarters full. But now and then I produce an unusually large haul of debris. On those occasions, I have to turn into a one-person compaction crew: I grab a low-hanging branch of the persimmon tree, hoist myself up, drop down feet-first into the can, and bounce around to squash everything enough to squeeze in the overflow. Consider this my audition to be your role model, Scorpio. According to my reading of the celestial weather, it’s time for you to consolidate and discard at least half a year’s accumulation of obsolete clutter—both the invisible emotional kind and the tangible stuff filling your space.

SAGITTARIUS (Nov. 22-Dec. 21): Ancient navigators sometimes crossed vast stretches of sea by studying the swells beneath their boats. Their bodies were instruments of perception that enabled them to feel the subtle wave patterns generated by winds and distant islands. Your intuition has a similar sensitivity these days, Sagittarius. I hope you will trust it: what your whole being senses before your rational mind assembles the evidence. I call this fully embodied intelligence. It deserves a key role in your decision-making.

CAPRICORN (Dec. 22-Jan. 19): I’ve never been a fan of Capricorn poet Kahlil Gibran (1883–1931). The ideas he expressed seem commonplace and sentimental to me. But his book *The Prophet* is an all-time bestseller translated into over 100 languages. Millions of readers have adored and benefited from his words, and he’s acclaimed as a literary hero in his native Lebanon. So who cares what I think! I’ll just shut up and appreciate the fact that he worked hard and published a lot. His disciplined, painstaking efforts have been widely inspirational. Let’s make him your role model for the coming months. I think you’re primed to create enduring offerings that nourish people’s souls.

AQUARIUS (Jan. 20-Feb. 18): Think of an aspect of your life that you have always wished you could change but have assumed or feared you could never change. What if, sometime soon, you try to change it, but this time you do it with playful lightheartedness? You resolve to feel zero stress and have as much fun as possible as you try to shift how this problem works. You decide you will use your imagination to dream up unprecedented and even outrageous ways to break your trance and invite sweet liberation to swoop in.

PISCES (Feb. 19-March 20): Geologists tell us that over time, rocks really do get transformed under sustained pressure. Their material gets reorganized into denser, more stable stuff. This is an apt metaphor for you, dear Pisces. You’re under pressure right now, and it may feel intense. But what if it’s actually reconfiguring you? Maybe the constraints are what you need to make you more focused, more essential, and more real. Not all pressure is bad, and this is proof. Ask yourself: What is this pressure making possible that freedom couldn’t create? Let yourself be reorganized.
Homework: Do you know how to turn one of your so-called liabilities into an asset ?

articles.title: Public Defenders Distance Themselves from Seattle City Attorney’s New Therapeutic Court
articles.author: Nathalie Graham
paras: Despite months of collaboration, the King County Department of Public Defense (DPD) has distanced itself from Seattle City Attorney Erika Evans’ new therapeutic court. The public defenders think Evans’ system, christened “connection court,” punishes repeat, low-level crime offenders and doesn’t do anything to solve the root problems of crime. That’s the same problem they have with the current system.

Seattle Municipal Court hasn’t had a community court, a therapeutic court where people can be connected with services rather than a jail sentence, since Republican Seattle City Attorney Ann Davison killed it in 2023 . On the campaign trail last year, all the Seattle city attorney candidates vowed to revive it (even Davison proposed a fucked up reimagined “drug court”).

In a matter of 10 months, Seattle City Attorney Erika has followed through on her promises. Sort of. Connection court, kicked off this week and will hear cases every other Wednesday, giving people same-day access to service connections. If they complete those “engagements” assigned by the court, their case will be dismissed.

Evans’ connection court has strict eligibility requirements, including a three-month period where anyone in connection court cannot commit another crime or they’ll be kicked from the program and have their case prosecuted the normal way. In another new program, Evans will also recommend “aggravated” sentences for repeat offenders.

As a candidate, Evans called for an “expansive” new community court that “reduces crime and recidivism” and allows “people who commit quality of life crimes to participate in the system.” Her platform didn’t mention recommending harsher sentences for repeat low-level offenders. When she took office , she said she would work with DPD on the new vision. Those conversations fell apart back in August, according to Katie Hurley, special counsel for criminal policy and practice at DPD.

“The current eligibility criteria for connection court, I would not characterize as ‘expansive,’” Hurley says, referring to Evans’ campaign platform. “I would characterize them as restrictive… more restrictive than we saw in the last iteration of community court.”

While Evans’ connection court bars anyone with serious criminal histories from entering the program (second degree assault convictions from the last two years, any rape or murder convictions), it also institutes a 90-day jurisdiction period where someone cannot break the law again. If they do, they’ll get booted out of connection court and have their case prosecuted normal-style. This is tough for people without homes who may receive criminal trespass charges for sleeping outside (connection court currently doesn’t connect people with shelter options, but Evans says she’s talking to Mayor Katie Wilson to set that up).

According to Hurley, the last iteration of Seattle’s community court had jurisdiction periods of 14 days or 28 days—long enough for a person to complete their “engagement,” or the task they were assigned by the community court, but not so long that they’d spend three months in purgatory with an open case.

Jenna Robert, criminal division chief in the City Attorney’s Office, explained that 90 days will give people time to finish their “engagements,” since connection court goes further than “check-the-box engagements.” Robert used an example of a mental health appointment—satisfying the engagement requirement would mean not just scheduling the appointment, but going to it. “The kind of thing we’re looking at is that extra step,” Robert says.
The 90-day jurisdiction period was the sticking point for DPD.

In mid-August, after months of discussions with Evans’ office and “shortly before the court had been initially scheduled to launch,” Hurley says, the CAO included the 90-day thing out of nowhere. DPD then distanced themselves from any association with connection court.
According to Evans, DPD wanted the jurisdiction period to be one day. “How can you think you can get someone what they need in one day?” Evans says.
Hurley clarified that DPD wanted the jurisdictional period to end and the connection court case to be finished once someone completed their engagements.
“If they were able to design exactly how they want it’s not exactly that, but it’s something better than not having it at all,” Evans says of DPD.

The other problem for DPD is Evans’ new High-Priority Repeat Offenses (HiPRO) program, which punishes anyone who has committed three crimes in three months or six crimes in six months by recommending “aggravated” sentences. It sounds a lot like her Republican predecessor Davison’s High-Utilizer Initiative, but Evans says it’s different. For one thing, unlike Davison’s “it’s not a list,” she says.

HiPRO “looks at conduct across a three-month-span,” Evans says. It also places special emphasis on crimes that impact businesses (trespassing, theft) and vehicle prowls. Those HiPRO cases aren’t eligible for connection court and face harsher recommended sentences.
But aggravated sentences will only occur after “we’ve given opportunity after opportunity,” Evans says.

“We’re talking about adding a slight aggravator to try to address that we’ve continued to give you these opportunities, and you’re not taking advantage of any of these off ramps,” Robert says. “We’re acknowledging that you’re disproportionately impacting the community, and we’re asking for that aggravator.”
Evans says it could look like a few extra days in jail, but it’s “not set in stone.”

For the DPD, this seems a lot like the current system: punishing repeat low-level crime offenders and not solving any of the root problems that cause crime. Those in HiPRO “are exactly the people who’ve been failed by the traditional system,” she says. Persistent low level behaviors that conventional prosecution hasn’t curbed are “precisely what connection court should be addressing and responding to.” Thinking added jail time can help is a sign of prosecutoritis.

Some of those people will still make it through connection court through “prosecutorial discretion,” Evans says. Or, they’ll be funneled into one of the numerous pre-file diversion programs. DPD remains skeptical.
While Evans is proud to have stood up connection court so quickly, she hopes it can expand. The current version “is not enough yet,” she says.

paras: Vance gleefully announced that the Trump administration is banning Microsoft from a green card program to recruit immigrant workers. Vance said, “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants.” Meanwhile, Microsoft is actually laying off employees as it shifts to AI , and thousands of jobs have been eliminated, but are Vance and Trump getting mad about AI and introducing any legislation to protect American workers from being replaced with AI? Of course not! They fucking LOVE AI! To them, AI is a white Christian American man and can do no wrong.

Americans are dying from measles , and the government might be trying to cover it up, says Sen. Patty Murray. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro says two people have died from measles in his state, but RFK Jr. thinks Shapiro’s staff “ fabricated ” the deaths. He says the two patients who died had measles, but it wasn’t measles that killed them. Murray says the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is going to take a closer look at how they’re defining measles deaths, but Murray rightfully asks , “What is the goal of that? In my mind it’s to obscure how many people are dying.” There have been 2,800 reported measles cases this year—the most in 30 years.

In response to the way the CDC’s handling measles and, well, everything, Murray launched the Public Health for America Working Group on Wednesday to “develop a blueprint to build America’s public health system stronger, more resilient, and insulated from political interference.” The group includes a bunch of super smart cookies with impressive backgrounds in everything from COVID-19 research and AIDS policy to a doctor who was dismissed from a CDC Advisory Committee when RFK Jr. came along.

And speaking of RFK Jr. , he’s one of those assholes who doesn’t believe HIV causes AIDS and I highly recommend listening to the latest episode of Maintenance Phase to learn more about the history of all those dangerous dummies. Like, they sincerely believe poppers and “bowls of antibiotics at sex parties” cause AIDS, and holy fuck this man is in charge of our nation’s health? His newest obsession is an initiative to address vaccine injury, including a billing code to “reimburse doctors for filing reports of serious vaccine side effects.” That’s corrupt as fuuuuuuck.
There’s a new Mars picture! The Curiosity rover took some pictures of dawn on Mars and it kind of looks like the Badlands. I fucking love the Badlands.

Two of the stores on the list—in Redmond and Spokane—are represented by the union.

Students are demonstrating in France again today , over public school conditions . This time around, college students are joining in after seeing how police used force against the young protestors last week. The New York Times reports, “Roughly 6,600 people have been arrested, according to the government, and some 760 police officers and over 300 students and school staff have been injured” since protests began. One college student told the paper, “We are used to seeing police in France beat people but they are normally adults. These are kids.”
Honestly, I’m proud of Gen Z. They’re protesting, they’re paying for music , they’re buying art . The kids are alright.

Want to live longer? Be a tortoise . The oldest land animal, Jonathan, is supposedly 194 years old, and scientists are studying him to see what they can learn about longevity. Jonathan has seen some shit! I bet he remembers what bananas used to taste like .

Christa Pike’s awake, pissed . As Charles shared in yesterday’s Slog AM, Pike, who survived a botched execution last week, is awake. Her lawyers say she has a “long road to recovery.” Her lawyer said “She has a blood clot in her arm and pneumonia. She can’t swallow, so she hasn’t eaten since the date of her execution. She can’t move her arms, and her limbs are ‘tremendously’ swollen. Her legal team said they’re unsure if she will recover function in those limbs.” Meanwhile, a judge has ordered the state to preserve all evidence relating to the execution. I hope she sues the pants off the state and Governor Bill Lee, who is an absolute chode.

Hello , I’m Cherry, I’m 14 and an aspiring film-maker. I love how your films capture what it feels like to be a young girl growing up. We hear so much about the famous men in your family, but how have the successful women in your family inspired and influenced you? Your films capture the experience of what it is to be a young girl in a way words often can’t. CherryEmma That’s nice to hear, thank you. I feel like I got a lot from my mom about being true to yourself, following what you’re interested in and seeing the beauty in your surroundings. My mom always noticed odd details in life, so a lot of my films are made up of those kinds of things.

Your films beautifully capture the isolation of hotel rooms – spaces completely detached from a character’s past or future. If you were forced into that stillness and could choose to preserve only one cherished memory while erasing another for ever, what would they be? Malpractice1 It’s hard to pick a memory, but recently we had a party in Versailles for the anniversary of Marie Antoinette and New Order played. When they started playing Ceremony [from the soundtrack] and the lights went on, I just know that in the future when I have to remember a happy memory, that’s going to be it. Even painful memories are part of making you who you are, and you learn from them, so I can’t think of anything I would erase.

articles.title: The woman with the mattress: the radical, rage-fuelled history of anti-rape art
articles.author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
paras: A performance piece from 2014 has gone viral in response to an allegation of rape at Cornell University. But with such defiant pieces stretching back hundreds of years, will things ever change?

In September 2014, Emma Sulkowicz began to carry a blue mattress weighing 23kg around her university campus. The mattress was similar to the ones New York’s Columbia University used in its dorm rooms, where Sulkowicz said she had been raped by a fellow student two years earlier. Her performance/endurance artwork constituted her visual art senior thesis, drawing attention to the lack of criminal charges brought against her alleged attacker and his continued presence at the university. As she hauled it across campus, others could choose to assist her with her burden. Many did. She recorded responses to the piece in a diary.

“I could have taken my pillow,” she told the writer Jessica Valenti at the time. “But I want people to see how it weighs down a person to be ignored by the school administration and harassed by police.” Sulkowicz would carry the mattress , she said, for as long as her alleged attacker remained at Columbia. And so she ended up carrying it all the way to graduation where, helped by other women, she took it on stage. The university president refused to shake her hand, turning away from her instead.

articles.title: A molecule’s ‘handedness’ can determine whether it’s an effective drug – 4 examples of pharmaceuticals where chirality matters
articles.author:
<name>Cedric Schaack, Assistant Professor of Chemistry, Wake Forest University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/cedric-schaack-2770043"/>
paras: The 2026 Nobel Prize in chemistry concerns a property called chirality, which may sound like an abstract science term but is actually all around you, all the time.

Picture a spiral galaxy rotating in space, or follow the outline of a snail’s shell as it spirals clockwise to the tip. In each case, you can draw a mirror image of the spiral that won’t overlap with the original picture.

You can even see this property on your own body: Hold out your hands, palms up. Your hands are mirror images of one another, yet however you turn them, you can never lay your right hand exactly on top of your left with both palms facing the same way.

All of these are examples of chirality . Chiral objects have a mirror image that cannot be superimposed directly on them. This concept shows up in geometry in the shapes of organisms and, most consequentially, in the molecules that make up living things. This week, the 2026 Nobel Prize in chemistry went to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for their work on how chemistry can favor one chiral version, or “hand,” over the other.

As chemists who design and measure chiral molecules, we work with this mirror-image problem every day. Molecular handedness has far-reaching implications , and you can see why when you consider how chiral objects interact with one another in daily life.

A regular claw hammer is an achiral, or nonchiral, tool. It works identically whether you hold it in your left hand or right hand. But a pair of scissors is often made to favor a right-handed user. If you are left-handed and have used right-handed scissors, you know the result: Squeezing them with your right hand pulls the blades inward against each other, while squeezing them with the left pushes the blades outward, so they fold the paper instead of cutting it. Scissors are chiral tools designed to interact with the human hand, which is also chiral.

Nearly every protein on Earth is built from one mirror-image form of each amino acid, and DNA and RNA from one form of sugars. DNA assembles to form helices of one, and only one, chirality. Similarly, snail shells almost always spiral in the same direction for every snail species. This omnipresent single-handedness of every known living thing is called homochirality .

When chemists make chiral molecules without adding any external chiral agents, they get a racemic mixture : an even 50:50 blend of both hands. So how did the primordial soup that formed life on Earth, which presumably had this exact balanced chemistry, end up one-handed?
This question remained open until the groundbreaking discoveries honored by the 2026 Nobel Prize in chemistry, awarded to Kagan and Soai.

In the 1980s, Kagan found that a catalyst, a helper that speeds up a reaction, does not have to be entirely made of molecules with the same handedness to make a purely single-handed product. In some reactions, a partly pure catalyst yielded a product purer than the catalyst itself.

In the 1990s, Soai found a molecule that makes copies of itself and favors its own hand over its mirror-image version. Start with a 51:49 imbalance, and after a few rounds the mixture is overwhelmingly one-handed. Later versions of the reaction amplified an imbalanced mixture of just 0.00005% to better than 99.5%.
While the Soai reaction is a laboratory system and not a recreation of early Earth, it shows one possibility for how life may have chosen one-handedness.

Because life evolved under homochirality, the human body is a highly chiral environment. Cell receptors and enzymes are built from single-handed proteins. Consequently, a pharmaceutical molecule enters the body like a key looking for its lock. If a drug is administered as a racemic mixture of both hands, one mirror image may fit the receptor perfectly, while its mirror twin doesn’t. This twin can trigger unintended side effects, or it may fit as a key into an entirely different enzyme and disrupt your body’s usual processes.

Throughout medical history, controlling chirality has meant the difference between therapeutic breakthroughs and medical tragedies. Chemists label the two mirror-image forms with letters, D and L for sugars and R and S for most drugs, so the letter tells you which version you’re holding. Four chiral molecules in particular can illustrate why handedness matters in medicine.

The first is thalidomide. Sold in the late 1950s as a 50:50 mixture to treat insomnia and morning sickness, thalidomide was widely prescribed in Europe, Canada and Australia. After its manufacturer withdrew it in 1961, more than 10,000 children were found to have been born with severe malformations, in which their limbs were shortened or failed to form.
A 1979 study in mice pointed to thalidomide’s S-form as the culprit . But thalidomide’s molecules are chemically flexible, meaning they can convert between the two forms while inside your body.
Even a purely single-handed version would not have been safe.
Another example is ibuprofen. Ibuprofen was developed at the British company Boots in the 1960s and has become one of the most widely used pain relievers in the world.
Ibuprofen’s S form does the work , blocking enzymes that produce chemical signals for pain and swelling. The R-form is largely inactive and does nothing against these signals.
Luckily, the body corrects the mix : An enzyme in your body converts a share of the R-form into the S-form, which is why a pill containing both forms works anyway.

A third example is L-DOPA. In 1969, neurologist Oliver Sacks gave L-DOPA to patients who had spent decades nearly motionless after the encephalitis epidemic of the early 20th century. Many patients woke up, spoke and moved in the episode later told in his book and the film “ Awakenings .” The effect proved largely temporary, but the drug remains a mainstay of Parkinson’s treatment.

In Parkinson’s disease, neurons producing a chemical messenger called dopamine degenerate, and the dopamine itself cannot cross from the bloodstream into the brain . L-DOPA can, and enzymes in the brain then convert it into dopamine.

Its mirror image, D-DOPA, is not a fit for that enzyme, so it does not make the transition. However, making only the L-form at scale was a challenge. In the 1970s, William Knowles at Monsanto solved this issue using a special chiral catalyst. This work earned him a share of the 2001 Nobel Prize in chemistry.

A final example is glucose. Corn or grape sugar is commonly known as glucose, but the term actually refers to specifically one form, called the D-enantiomer, of this sugar. Cells run on D-glucose. The first step of glycolysis , the chain of reactions cells use to pull energy out of sugar, uses an enzyme that recognizes only that form.

Its mirror image, L-glucose, has the same physical properties, such as melting point, appearance and sweet taste. Yet, cellular enzymes cannot process it, so it supplies no calories and does not raise your blood sugar. In the 1980s, researchers explored it as a low-calorie sweetener for people with diabetes, but high production costs made it financially unviable.

Handedness matters well beyond the body. Chiral molecules emit and absorb light that is circularly polarized , meaning it twists to the left or right as it travels. Researchers are developing displays that produce this type of light directly, which could be used to make screens that work in very bright environments, such as direct sunlight.

The same property is useful for security. A tag made with chiral molecules can look like an ordinary mark in normal light but reveal a hidden pattern through a filter that passes only left-twisting or right-twisting light. This property could make it harder to counterfeit.

Chirality also shapes how electrons move. Electrons have a built-in property called spin , which you can picture as a tiny compass needle pointing up or down. When electrons pass through chiral molecules, one type of spin can get through more easily than others. Because spin can carry information, controlling it could lead to electronics that waste less energy and to new quantum devices, although scientists are still debating how the effect works.
Kagan’s and Soai’s work showed how a faint asymmetry between two chiral forms can grow into a decisive preference. Chemists are learning to build that preference into materials, not just medicines.
