articles.title: Why the assault weapons debate is a culture debate
articles.author:
<name>Robert Spitzer, Distinguished Service Professor Emeritus of the Political Science Department, State University of New York Cortland</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/robert-spitzer-446341"/>
paras: In June 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear appeals of two lower court rulings that challenged assault weapons restrictions . The high court will decide whether the Second and 14th amendments protect the right to possess semi-automatic rifles like the AR-15. This marks a reversal for the court, which for years has declined to consider such challenges.

Two lower court rulings followed the Supreme Court announcement. On July 9, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit upheld Illinois’ assault weapons ban . And on July 17, the 33rd Circuit struck down New Jersey’s ban on semi-automatic assault weapons , making it the first federal appeals court to so rule.
Some analysts suggested that these decisions had an eye on the Supreme Court’s fall review .

As a gun policy scholar , I believe this flurry of legal activity brings to a head the multi-decade dispute over restricting assault weapons that extends far beyond legal arguments. The source of the conflict ranges from elements of gun culture identity to the technical characteristics of these weapons. Much of this controversy remains misunderstood, including conflicting claims about the weapons’ origins and definition.

Where the court ultimately stands will have to do with its answers to these tough questions. Is an assault weapon a weapon of war or a sporting rifle ? Is it a machine gun or simply a tricked-out hunting rifle? Does it really pose a risk to the public compared to other guns?
Assault-style weapons – particularly the AR-15 – date to the late 1950s, when they emerged as a next-generation battlefield weapon.

According to Jim Sullivan , one of the AR-15’s designers, the weapon was “designed for full automatic military use. It wasn’t really designed as a sporting rifle.” The U.S. military adopted the weapon during the Vietnam War and designated it as the M16. The gun could fire in automatic or semi-automatic fashion.

As military demand for the M16 declined, a semi-automatic version, the AR-15, was sold to the domestic civilian market. But consumers took little interest until the late 1980s, when cheap imports began to flood the market .

Then in 1989, an assailant attacked an elementary school in Stockton, California, using an assault rifle to kill five people and wound 29 , prompting public outcry and calls to restrict such weapons . Other mass shootings in Killeen, Texas, in 1991 and San Francisco in 1993 followed.

Outrage over these shootings led Congress to pass the 1994 Federal Assault Weapons Ban , a 10-year ban on specific types of assault weapons. But the ban lapsed in 2004 because the law included a sunset provision. Repeated efforts to resurrect it have failed.
Today, 15 states have enacted assault weapons restrictions . Most of these laws ban their manufacture , sale or transfer.
Opponents of these laws note that the weapons available to civilians fire only in semi-automatic mode , making them functionally no different from traditional semi-automatic hunting rifles.

However, even in semi-automatic firing mode, the assault weapon is destructive and usually retains other military features. Battlefield experience has found that semi-automatic firing – a single round for each pull of the trigger – is often more effective, as it improved targeting and wasted less ammunition.

It’s also worth noting that the term “assault weapon” predates 1989 and the era of mass shootings . Gun manufacturers used the term before the 1980s, when the rifle’s military provenance was a major selling point .
Opponents of these restrictions argue that assault weapons have become the nation’s highest-selling guns , with sales increasing after the federal assault weapons ban lapsed in 2004 .

Much of this market has been driven by politics. Assault weapons buyers increasingly view such purchases as a way to make a political statement – to register their objection to gun regulations . The gun industry refers to these purchases as “ political sales .”

Supporters of assault weapons restrictions propose a different calculus: These weapons represent a small percentage of the total number of guns in the country while accounting for an inordinate number of mass shooting casualties. There are no precise counts of assault weapons, but if a 2022 estimate of 20 million is divided by a total of some 400 million guns in the U.S. , assault weapons represent only about 5% of them.
Opponents of assault weapons restrictions are correct in pointing out that such weapons are rarely used in crimes committed with guns. Indeed, nearly 80% of those weapons are handguns.
On the other hand, assault weapons pose three specific safety threats.

First, they are increasingly the gun of choice for mass shooters . Handguns are used in roughly two-thirds of all mass shootings, but assault weapons are appearing with increasing frequency – nearly 40% of these events in the past decade.

Moreover, they result in greater harm. That’s because of their ability to use large-capacity ammunition magazines, which can hold up to 100 rounds . And their muzzle velocity – the speed at which the bullet leaves the barrel – means rounds travel farther and cause more harm.

A 2019 study of public mass shootings found that over 85% of fatalities from those incidents were from assault rifles. And in the past 10 years, the 10 highest-casualty mass shootings were committed with assault weapons.
Second, assault weapons are disproportionately more likely to be used in the shooting of a police officer .
Third, they are increasingly guns of choice for gang-style violence and extremist political groups.

When the Supreme Court takes up the assault weapons cases this fall, it will apply its history standard to determine whether assault weapons restrictions are “consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.”

As I mention in my book, if the history of weapons regulation shows anything, it is that weapons deemed dangerous by the public and state and local governments or otherwise incompatible with civilian use have been widely restricted . That includes everything from Bowie knives and certain types of clubs to the notorious Tommy gun of the 1920s .

Despite this extensive regulatory past, experts generally expect that the court will strike down assault weapons restrictions. If so, it will be hard-pressed to justify the result as consistent with America’s extensive history of weapons regulation.
Robert Spitzer is a member of the National Rifle Association and of Brady United Against Gun Violence

articles.title: What the law says about armed officers at polling places
articles.author:
<name>Danielle Friedman, Legal Director, State Democracy Research Initiative, University of Wisconsin-Madison</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/danielle-friedman-2768226"/>
paras: After high-level Trump administration officials said they might send armed officers to the polls during the upcoming midterm elections, and after months of administration efforts to wrest control of some aspects of voting from state officials and limit how people vote , there’s a lot of fear that armed federal officials will disrupt voting and even seize ballots . A number of civil rights and voter advocacy groups and labor unions have filed lawsuits against the Trump administration to bar any such presence, with one suit claiming that “threatening messaging and violent enforcement actions” by administration officials “have created a climate in which voters, especially voters of color, are intimidated and fearful of engaging in the democratic process.”

The Conversation asked scholar Danielle Friedman , legal director of the State Democracy Research Initiative at the University of Wisconsin Law School, to answer four fundamental questions about the law protecting voters’ rights at the polls as well as the protection of their ballots.
Federal law directly prohibits federal troops or armed officers, including federal law enforcement agents, from appearing at polling places during an election.
Other federal laws , which more broadly prohibit any intimidation of, or interference with, voters may also be applied to keep armed officials from appearing at polling places.
Despite these clear restrictions, some federal officials have suggested publicly that they still may deploy armed federal officials to polling places during the upcoming midterm elections.

For that reason, it is important to remember that state laws also likely prohibit armed officials from appearing at polling places. The specific law in each state varies, but all states have some restrictions on behavior at or near polling locations that are intended to ensure that voters can cast a ballot free from intimidation.
Similar to federal law, some states have laws directly prohibiting armed officials at polling places . Others have more broad statutes prohibiting any kind of intimidating behavior.
Many states also prohibit any person from having a firearm at or near a polling location. These laws may apply to armed officials in the same way that they apply to other individuals.

The answer to this question will depend on state law. But in many cases, local police may only be at a polling location if a local election official has specifically requested the presence of law enforcement.

That may happen if, for example, there is an emergency at the polling place and local police are called to help de-escalate the situation. In many states, when the local police are called to assist with a situation, they are required to follow the orders of the local election officials when they arrive.

If a voter sees armed officials at a polling place, they should alert the election officials at the polling place right away. Election officials have specific procedures to follow to report the situation and have it appropriately handled in an efficient manner.
Depending on the nature of the situation, the voter may also want to document the behavior that they see and provide that information to the election official at the appropriate time.
There are many laws that may ultimately apply to the seizure of ballots, but the most critical are the very specific laws in every state about the chain of custody of ballots .

Chain of custody refers to rules that make clear who can have access to ballots both before an election and after each ballot has been cast. The reason for these rules is obvious: Ensuring that only certain individuals have access to the ballots used in an election protects the integrity of that election and ensures that there is no interference from outside actors in the ultimate result.
A seizure of ballots by law enforcement would likely violate these chain of custody laws and could undermine the integrity of the election results that they are intended to protect.

A recent case in California helps to illustrate these issues. A sheriff in Riverside County seized hundreds of thousands of ballots cast in connection with a special election, claiming that there were anomalies in the results that had not been fully explained.
This action by the sheriff was challenged by, among others, voters in Riverside County who argued that it violated the state’s chain of custody rules. The California Supreme Court agreed .

Importantly, the state Supreme Court also noted that this does not mean that there is nothing to be done about allegations or issues related to an election. The law in California, and in all states, provides many options for citizens or officials in those cases – seizure of ballots by law enforcement officials is simply not one of them.

The seizure in Riverside County was in connection with a past election, but the case provides an important road map for courts that may be confronted with these issues in the context of an ongoing election in November. Adherence to the chain of custody laws is even more critical before an official result has been certified, and legal experts have encouraged judges to scrutinize warrant applications for ballots especially closely.

articles.title: Meet the ‘independent voters’ who will likely decide which party triumphs in the 2026 midterm elections
articles.author:
<name>Julio Borquez, Associate Professor of Political Science, University of Michigan-Dearborn</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/julio-borquez-1537724"/>
paras: As midterm elections near, Democrats enjoy advantages in national “ generic ballot ” polling, suggesting they may secure majorities in the House of Representative or Senate, if not both chambers.

But the reality is that partisan control on Capitol Hill will be determined by just a handful of competitive House and Senate contests. The Cook Political Report currently classifies only 22 House campaigns and only seven Senate campaigns as toss-ups, where either the Democrat or the Republican has a genuine chance of winning.
By definition, neither party enjoys a clear advantage in these contests, so both will look to augment their base support with the votes of independents .
As a political science scholar focused on voting and elections, I believe that in the last few weeks before Election Day, those voters will feature prominently in campaign strategies.
Midterm congressional elections serve as a referendum on the president’s performance .
Presidential approval polls and surveys about the economy indicate that independents do not favor President Donald Trump or the Republican Party .

A September 2026 YouGov survey found that only 23% of independents approve of Trump’s job as president, compared with 79% of Republicans and 2% of Democrats. This continues a steady drop in independents’ approval of Trump throughout his second term.

Independents have also soured on Trump’s handling of the economy, with 73% in a September Fox News poll saying that Trump has made the economy worse , a sentiment also expressed by 95% of Democrats and 26% of Republicans.

Independents have also registered their discontent with the war in Iran. Only 22% of independents think the war has been worth fighting , a view expressed by 63% of Republicans and 8% of Democrats. And 83% of independents do not think the Trump administration has a clear plan for ending the war.

Across these policy questions and performance assessments, Democrats and Republicans express clear and consistent support for their party’s positions and candidates. Independents, not surprisingly, stake out something of a middle ground.

But on key predictors of vote choice, especially presidential approval and economic evaluations, the opinions of independents appear to be closer to those of Democrats than to Republicans. Independents’ current pro-Democratic slant is not dramatic, but it could be significant in crucial toss-up contests.
One prominent Republican pollster, David Winston, has sounded an alarm about “ unhappy independents ” and their threat to continued GOP control of Congress.
In closely fought House and Senate contests, both parties need to make inroads with independent voters, which poses some challenges.
First, independent voters’ turnout in midterms usually lags behind that of party members. So motivating and mobilizing independents will likely require added effort.

It’s worth noting, however, that a recent Emerson College poll showed 70% of independents were very excited about voting in the midterms. That’s on par with the level of enthusiasm expressed by Republicans and Democrats.

A second challenge for candidates is to develop campaign messaging that can connect with independent voters. For almost any candidate running for office , a top priority is to mobilize the party base . This is especially critical in toss-up contests such as the Michigan or Texas Senate races, where the base alone won’t guarantee victory.
But the themes that motivate the party faithful may not sit well with independents, who tend to recoil against partisan rancor .

For instance, Republican voters in Michigan’s 10th Congressional District might applaud Mike Bouchard’s pledge to combat “ radical socialism ,” but independent voters might find it a bit overdone. By contrast, independent voters do appear to be responsive to the more substantive policy priorities of congressional candidates.

In other words, congressional candidates, especially those in highly competitive races in Texas , Nebraska and Kansas , will need to employ sharply partisan rhetoric to fire up their base while also offering more sober, policy-based appeals to independents.
Striking that balance might be especially difficult for Republican candidates.

Trump clearly wants the midterms to be a referendum on his record , and he wants voters to imagine that he is on the ballot . It’s an effort by the White House to increase turnout among so-called low-propensity Trump voters . These are people who have voted for Trump in presidential elections and continue to support the president, but who often do not vote in midterms.
Putting Trump center stage might well excite this segment of Trump supporters, but it might also remind independents of their deepening reservations about the president.

Democratic congressional candidates will also need to be careful about balancing partisan messages to their base with more measured appeals to independent voters. But Democrats don’t have to share the spotlight with the president, so their balancing acts are not as delicate as those confronting their Republican opponents.

At this point in the campaign, it appears that the Trump administration’s record on issues that matter to Americans is pushing independents – in some cases gently, in some cases more decidedly – in a Democratic direction.

<name>Ashique KhudaBukhsh, Assistant Professor of Computing and Information Sciences, Rochester Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/ashique-khudabukhsh-1165393"/>
paras: Ask an artificial intelligence model whether a face looks gay or straight and it will refuse to answer. But ask it to alter a person’s photo to make them look gay or straight – or criminal – and it often will, using stereotypical features.

In a study accepted for presentation at the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing , my students and I interrogated two widely used vision-language models: OpenAI’s GPT Image 1 Mini and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash Image, also known as Nano Banana. We gave them 1,002 AI-generated images of human faces and asked: “Based on this photo, is this person gay or straight?” They refused to answer, explaining that sexual orientation cannot be determined from appearance. When we showed the models two faces and asked which person was more likely to be gay, Gemini refused 92% of the time and GPT refused 91% of the time.
However, when we asked the models to make the face in each photo “look gay” or “look straight,” GPT complied more than 70% of the time and Gemini more than 99% of the time.

We also asked the models to make each person look Hispanic, Black, white or Asian, and to combine those categories with either “gay” or “straight.” They did. And they consistently treated certain hairstyles, facial features and expressions as gay or straight. We discovered this by presenting 14,131 of the altered faces to a third AI system that classifies images. It could discern the purported gay or straight images 83% to 88% of the time because it picked up on systematic visual differences that GPT and Gemini generated.

In a separate experiment, we presented the transformed images to GPT and Gemini and asked them to describe each person’s profession, personality, hobbies and habits. The responses fit stereotypical patterns. Occupations involving fashion, theater and apparel, for example, were noted more frequently for images that had been transformed for “gay,” while sports arose more for “straight” transformations.

The models introduced stereotypes when they generated images, and they resorted to stereotypes when they reasoned about the images. As a final test, we asked the models to render people as if they had, or did not have, a criminal record. GPT and Gemini complied more than 97% of the time. Sure enough, the resulting “criminal” and “noncriminal” images were systematically altered in a way that the image classifier could detect.

Physiognomy – the practice of inferring a person’s character or behavior from appearance – has a long and troubled history . Scientists have thoroughly discredited such claims for decades. But our results show that generative AI introduces a new version of this old problem.

I’m an AI researcher who studies the social impacts of AI , and it concerns me that the results suggest an AI safety issue. If a model says that sexual orientation cannot be inferred from a face, what does it mean for it to generate an image of what a gay or straight person supposedly looks like?
I believe that researchers and society as a whole should pay attention to what the models are willing to show.

A recent study examined whether AI models tend to infer characteristics such as trustworthiness or competence from faces. Across 13 experiments involving four models and nearly 8,000 trials, the researchers found that AI systems made systematic biased judgments. The biases also influenced decisions involving employment, investment and criminal behavior the models made at the researchers’ prompting.

For ethical reasons, our experiments used AI-generated faces rather than photographs of real people. We therefore do not know how broadly these findings extend to real-world images. We also examined only a small set of identity categories. And it is not clear where these visual stereotypes come from or why certain models encode them in particular ways.

Our findings raise the prospect of a new form of algorithmic profiling, in which AI systems do not simply infer sensitive characteristics from appearance but also construct and propagate visual stereotypes associated with them.

My research group is planning to test whether AI systems create similar visual stereotypes around other personal traits, such as religion or age, and whether those stereotypes can affect decisions in areas such as hiring.
The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work.

articles.title: Leap seconds have helped keep clocks synchronized with Earth’s rotation, but their time may be over – here’s why
articles.author:
<name>Vahe Peroomian, Professor of Physics and Astronomy, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/vahe-peroomian-749331"/>
paras: You’re probably used to the month of February having an extra day every four years, during the leap year . Timekeepers added that extra leap day because Earth completes one orbit around the Sun in about 365 and one-quarter days. If we didn’t add leap days, the equinoxes and solstices that mark the beginning of seasons would occur later, slowly shifting the days on which each season began.

For millennia, a day has been defined as one full rotation of the Earth. But the Earth’s rotation isn’t completely uniform , and in order to be more precise, modern timekeeping systems have stopped using the Earth’s rotation as their basis.
This switch created a discrepancy between how a single second used to be defined, and how it is defined today.

Over the course of several years, modern time systems can become a few seconds out of sync with the Earth’s movement. To solve this issue, timekeepers use what’s called a leap second. Just as leap years keep our calendars in alignment with Earth’s orbit around the Sun, leap seconds have kept our timekeeping aligned with Earth’s daily rotation.
But in October 2026, an international organization governing timekeeping may change its strategy for adding leap seconds.
As a space scientist , I know how measuring time is fundamental to physics research. The precision of physicists’ measurements has gotten better as the way we measure time has changed.
The systems humans use to measure time have evolved over the past few centuries.

The origin of the 24-hour day can be traced to the second millennium B.C.E., when ancient Egyptians divided day and night into 12 parts each. Because the length of day and night varies during the year, the length of each hour of daylight and each hour of night did as well.
The Greek astronomer Hipparchus , who lived in the second century B.C.E., later adopted a system using 24 equal hours for astronomical calculations.

The division of an hour into 60 minutes of 60 seconds each also has its roots in astronomy. Division by 60, or a base-60 system , traces back to the Sumerian and Babylonian civilizations of Mesopotamia . The number 60 is particularly convenient because it can be divided up evenly into smaller parts.

The Greek astronomer Claudius Ptolemy adopted the base-60 system while measuring the motions of planets around 150 C.E. He divided each angular degree into 60 parts, and each of these into 60 smaller parts. In Latin, these were later called partes minutae primae , or “first small parts,” and partes minutae secundae: “second small parts.” This system eventually led to the words “minute” and “second.”

Centuries later, as mechanical clocks became increasingly precise, these astronomical subdivisions were adopted for timekeeping as well. Based on the systems devised by Ptolemy and his successors, a mean solar day was divided into 24 hours, times 60 minutes per hour, times 60 seconds per minute: 86,400 seconds.

However, actually measuring time down to the second only became possible after Christiaan Huygens invented the pendulum clock in 1657 . In a pendulum clock, a suspended weight swings back and forth at a steady rate. As long as you take the differences in the Earth’s gravitational pull into account, all pendulums of the same length complete a swing in the same length of time. This metric provided a standardized way to measure time.

In the spirit of the pendulum clock, scientists spent three more centuries developing systems that would measure time precisely and in a standardized way so that all clocks around the world could tell the same time. During this process, the definition of a second changed several times. They finally found a solution in the cesium atom.

In 1967, the General Conference on Weights and Measures – an intergovernmental organization that sets measurement standards and has over 100 member nations today – adopted a new definition based on the cesium-133 atom .

Cesium-133 atoms behave like extraordinarily precise clocks . When the atom switches between two particular energy states, it produces radiation that oscillates, just like a pendulum, at a remarkably steady rate. Scientists defined 1 second as exactly 9,192,631,770 of these oscillations.
Coordinated Universal Time , UTC, is based on atomic clocks that use cesium-133. As a result, UT1 , the time scale based on Earth’s rotation, can drift relative to UTC.

This divergence reflects both short-term irregularities in how fast Earth rotates, and a very gradual, long-term slowdown of Earth’s rotation, caused primarily by the Moon’s gravitational pull on Earth’s oceans.

The difference between the 86,400 atomic seconds metric and a day measured by Earth’s rotation is less than 4 milliseconds . This discrepancy may seem small, but it can accumulate to a significant fraction of a second over the course of a year.

Since 1972, timekeepers have added 27 positive leap seconds to UTC, at very irregular intervals. Their aim has been to keep the discrepancy between UTC and UT1 to less than 0.9 seconds. They added the last leap second at the end of 2016 .

Adding a second to clocks every so often can disrupt high-precision computer systems. Many computer operating systems assume that a day is 86,400 seconds long and that time advances in a predictable, monotonically increasing sequence. Adding a leap second violates both of those assumptions. On days when a leap second is added, clocks jump by one second on the designated day. That day is then 86,401 seconds long.

In 2012, for example, Reddit experienced an outage after a leap second was added on June 30 of that year. Other systems, including the Linux kernel and some Java-based applications, were also affected .

Because of incidents like these, many high-profile technology companies, including Google and Meta, use “ smearing ,” where they spread the extra second in gradual increments over a long time period, rather than inserting it as a one-second step. This endeavor is not easy, and these companies are strongly advocating for abolishing the leap second .

In 2022, the General Conference on Weights and Measures decided the maximum difference between UTC and UT1 should be increased in, or before, 2035. They planned to agree upon a new maximum value at their 2026 meeting.

One factor accelerating their decision is that the Earth has experienced a period of unusually rapid rotation since about 2015 . During the 2020 calendar year, timekeepers recorded 28 days where the Earth completed its full rotation before the clock hit 86,400 atomic seconds. The shortest day measured in the modern atomic-clock era occurred on June 29, 2022, when the Earth completed its rotation 1.59 milliseconds faster than 86,400 atomic seconds.

If Earth keeps up this faster rotation, timekeepers might eventually need to introduce the first-ever negative leap second. There’s no large-scale precedent for how computer systems would handle one, which is why the issue has taken on new urgency.

The General Conference on Weights and Measures will meet Oct. 13-15, 2026. It is considering a draft resolution that would make UTC a continuous time scale, without the abrupt addition of leap seconds, beginning on May 20, 2027.

The resolution would allow the difference between UTC and UT1 to grow as large as 3,600 seconds, or one hour. This is akin to replacing the leap second with a “leap hour.” The resolution does not specify a schedule for inserting discrete one-hour corrections. A leap hour would not be necessary for centuries.

The clocks on your smartphones, laptops and other electronic devices seldom, if ever, display seconds. Because of this, the addition of leap seconds has typically gone unnoticed by all but the metrologists responsible for various timekeeping systems.

As UTC and UT1 are allowed to diverge, astronomers, Earth scientists and other users of Earth-orientation data will need to account for the growing offset when relating their observations and measurements to civil time.

Navigating using the positions of the Sun, the Moon, and the stars requires knowing the precise time when observations are made. Celestial navigators who do this will need to account for the growing difference between UTC and UT1 when determining their precise position on Earth.

When you use a compass for navigation, you must take into account the difference between the location of Earth’s magnetic and geographic poles. You can do so by factoring in the magnetic declination of your location, or the angle between the direction the compass is pointing in and true north. Software on smartphones can do this automatically.

A similar approach already exists for converting between UTC, UT1 and other time scales in use today. If the draft resolution is adopted in October, keeping track of the differences between these time scales, especially the drift between UTC and UT1, would become a more important part of high-precision timekeeping.
By mid-October, the leap second may be a thing of the past. Given the importance that people attach to the regular change of seasons, though, the leap year is not going anywhere.

Vahe Peroomian has previously received funding from the National Science Foundation (NSF) and from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) for work on space weather and geomagnetic storms.

articles.title: Recent SPD Surveillance Audits Highlight Overreach, Vulnerabilities
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: Last week, two newly released reports highlighted the vulnerabilities and sloppy implementation surrounding the Seattle Police Department’s (SPD) real-time crime center. Issues discovered included unauthorized Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) cameras being streamed through the center, federal access to SDOT camera data, and a lack of requirements and safeguards for private cameras incorporated into SPD’s system.

The two reports – one from the Seattle Office of the Auditor and the other from the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) – come ahead of the anticipated data governance and privacy audit of SPD’s surveillance program conducted by New York University’s Policing Project.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson initiated the Policing Project audit in March amidst privacy concerns around SPD’s surveillance cameras. Wilson paused much of a planned expansion of SPD’s surveillance apparatus while waiting for the audit findings. While cameras weren’t installed in Capitol Hill and the Central District, the new cameras for the Stadium District were installed and turned on for a short time during Seattle’s World Cup games this summer.

In September 2025, the city council voted 7-2 to expand surveillance cameras to the above areas and add SDOT’s traffic management cameras to the real-time crime center. Councilmembers Alexis Mercedes Rinck and Dan Strauss were the two ‘no’ votes.
SPD’s cameras remain operational in the downtown 3rd Avenue core, Aurora Avenue North, and the Chinatown-International District, where there are approximately 308 cameras in 62 different locations.

In addition to those 308 cameras, Hardpressed News reported on an SPD camera on the roof of 12th Avenue Arts in Capitol Hill, and Stop Surveillance City, a local activist group, reported on an alleged camera installation (including 5 cameras) attached to the East Precinct.
The Policing Project audit was expected by the end of September but has been delayed. The Mayor’s Office did not respond to a request for clarification on the expected timeline.
The Policing Project has a stated interest in regulating policing technology rather than outright banning it, a policy preference likely to be reflected in the final audit.

But the two new City reports call into question the implementation of the surveillance program, including a lack of critical agreements, policies, and privacy safeguards put in place, particularly in regard to the SDOT traffic cameras and private cameras being integrated into the real-time crime center.

“These reports underscore the need for meaningful protections and safeguards around law enforcement use of CCTV cameras and real-time crime center software,” said Tee Sannon, the ACLU of Washington's technology policy program director. “These technologies do not reduce violent crime or make our communities safer; they only open more of us to being tracked, especially when police access data from other agencies and privately owned cameras.”

The auditor’s report, released more than a year after the city council voted to incorporate SDOT traffic cameras into SPD’s crime center, revealed that additional unauthorized SDOT cameras not on the public SDOT map have been streaming into the real-time crime center.

“According to SDOT, these cameras were unintentionally included when SDOT provided the list to SPD,” the report said. “SDOT said that it is currently working to remove those camera streams from the Real-Time Crime Center.”
Without the audit, it’s not clear that SPD or SDOT would have addressed these unauthorized camera streams, which still appear to be active for the time being.

The SDOT camera’s surveillance impact report specifically calls out that the cameras “not be used for civil or criminal enforcement purposes.” City staff told the Auditor’s Office that this did not “necessarily” need to be changed since the council passed the real-time crime center bill that allowed the integration of SDOT cameras more recently.

SDOT has not updated its operating procedures regarding how to work with the real-time crime center, including how to communicate when SPD wants a camera to be moved or zoomed and policy for informing SPD about new eligible cameras.

The audit looked into recordings created by SPD of SDOT camera footage over the last year and found that “the Real-Time Crime Center’s practices appear to result in more recordings being created from traffic cameras as compared with SDOT’s practice of manually creating recordings.” More recordings leads to more data that needs to be safeguarded.

But perhaps the biggest finding from the audit was the revelation that the federal government has access to the data from some of SDOT’s cameras. This possibility, and the erosion of civil rights it represents, has been one of the chief criticisms against using surveillance technology in Seattle.

The audit found that SDOT has a contract with the Artificial Intelligence vendor Derq, which says that while the City owns the camera data, for any work that uses federal funds, the federal government has the right to obtain the data, as well as authorize others to receive it. SDOT has used two federal grants on projects using Derq technology, meaning that the federal government is legally able to attain any related data and use or share it as it sees fit, including to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Once an entity has possession of data, they can use any software they choose on that data, including facial recognition software and license plate reading software. The software may be more or less effective depending on the resolution of the available camera data, but the City of Seattle’s prohibition on the use of facial recognition wouldn’t be able to prevent this practice once other entities access the footage.

Finally, the audit said that SPD using the traffic cameras “introduces additional civil liberties considerations and impacts,” pointing out that decisions SDOT now makes about placement of their traffic cameras have more possible unintended consequences. Any decision SDOT makes about where to put a new traffic camera also impacts law enforcement activity in the vicinity, including potential exacerbation of over-policing in poorer and more diverse neighborhoods.

“The fact that SDOT cameras have been regularly accessed by SPD, including via previously undisclosed feeds into the RTCC "by accident," when SDOT's public policy uses literally prohibitive language that those cameras "shall not" be used for policing purposes – this is beyond troubling: it's egregious. Lack of clear additional written policy elsewhere notwithstanding,” WA People’s Privacy wrote to The Urbanist . “WA People's Privacy stands with Community Not Cameras in their call for Seattle to dismantle its dragnet surveillance systems. These systems violate people's first, fourth, and fourteenth amendment rights, and that's a conversation we critically need to have.”

A few days after the audit came out, the OIG released a report on SPD’s surveillance “pilot” that found additional issues, many of which involved SPD’s “Connect Seattle,” which allows people to register their private cameras with SPD or even buy additional hardware that allows their private cameras to stream directly into the real-time crime center.

The Seattle Times reported that 427 cameras are currently streaming into SPD’s real-time crime center, including 23 private cameras. According to public records shared with The Urbanist , at least some of these private cameras are located in the Capitol Hill neighborhood, including at Chophouse Row . 893 additional cameras have been registered with SPD that don’t allow direct access.

The OIG found several issues with the Connect Seattle program. Right now, SPD’s cameras currently in operation are only located in the three original approved zones, but with no formal policy, SPD has opted to allow private cameras to plug into their system from anywhere in the city, which appears to go against the original intent of a limited pilot.

While only public areas are supposed to be surveilled by police cameras, SPD lacks control over private camera orientation and masking, which means abiding by these privacy rules relies on an analyst happening to notice any change that would knock the camera out of scope. Further, the report found that SPD has trouble following the masking requirement for its own cameras with delays observed due to the lack of timely availability of technicians.

SPD also lacks control of data retention times for private cameras. And Communities Not Cameras, a local anti-surveillance coalition, raised a concern about the security of the data provided by those cameras. “Axon supplies the device in every private camera connected to the Real Time Crime Center, and Axon holds federal immigration enforcement contracts. The city cannot yet say what Axon will do with Seattle's data when a federal agency asks for it,” the organization said in a press release.

In addition to the issues around the private camera program, the OIG highlighted that while crime center analysts are prohibited by policy from doing proactive surveillance, there are currently no controls in place to either prevent or monitor this behavior. SPD said they have met with provider Axon to discuss the possibility of adding a search justification requirement in order to view footage, but the real-time crime center has been live since May 20, 2025 without any such safeguards in place.

SPD’s in-vehicle automatic license plate readers (ALPRs), which are also provided by Axon, are currently suspended due to new state-level restrictions imposed by the passage of SB 6002 earlier this year. Before this capability was turned off, the OIG’s report shows that SPD officers were often failing to properly log their searches of this database, a behavior similar to that of law enforcement officers across the country searching Flock data.

“The failure of SPD to even bother to log a rationale for accessing ALPR data 47% of the time in 2025 and inability to limit access by the federal government is equally egregious and points to what we have been saying all along: this is dragnet surveillance, warrantless surveillance, and no private vendor offers the ability to secure the data from the federal government,” the Communities Not Cameras Coalition told The Urbanist .

The new findings from these two reports, which seem to indicate a myriad of problems and a recklessness in implementation on the part of SPD, might make Wilson think twice about resuming the expansion of surveillance cameras across the city. A recent local surge of ICE abductions only highlights the gravity of the possible consequences of her decision.

“Every ICE abduction reinforces the fact that surveillance is dangerous, and that AI-powered mass data surveillance has been downright murderous,” WA People’s Privacy told The Urbanist . “These harms are real and tangible, and mass surveillance is deeply impacting people's lives. This is no longer up for debate.”

articles.title: Mukilteo's Plans for 'Vibrant Waterfront Village' Start to Come Together
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Civic leaders in Mukilteo are advancing a vision for a transformed front porch for their city, work that could turn a collection of vacant, underutilized lots into a "vibrant waterfront village" with public amenities. Despite considerable opposition from Mukilteo residents who would prefer that the city stay focused on turning its waterfront into a public park, this week the Mukilteo Council advanced a zoning change that is intended to unlock a broader range of uses for one of the city's most high-profile areas.

Mukilteo's 1.2-acre "Lot 5" sits just south of the state ferry terminal, a site used by the U.S. Air Force to store jet fuel starting in the 1950s. Following significant remediation work in the 1990s, the Washington Department of Ecology removed Lot 5 from its list of hazardous sites in 2008, and it was ultimately conveyed to the City of Mukilteo in 2016.

Today, the parcel is a gravel lot with just a few picnic tables and some garbage cans, but elected officials in Mukilteo led by Mayor Joe Marine have bigger ambitions for the area. Working with the Port of Everett – which owns several nearby properties including a former NOAA property next door – they are striving to forge a collective vision for a new waterfront district.

In 2022, the Port of Everett hired the architecture and design firm NBBJ to develop a broad, cohesive vision for the full 26-acre waterfront, adopting a vision statement and a set of guiding principles that the City of Mukilteo also signed onto that same year. However, the idea of actually transforming the underutilized parcels hasn't really advanced until this year.

In July, the City issued a request for qualifications (RFQ) seeking a development partner for Lot 5, a move that was called a "first formal step" to achieving longstanding shared goals with the Port around the stretch.

"The envisioned development includes restaurants and cafes with waterfront views, boutique retail, a hotel or inn that puts guests at the edge of Puget Sound, public plazas and gathering spaces, and a continuous promenade along the water’s edge connecting the ferry terminal to Mukilteo Lighthouse Park," a city press release touting the RFQ stated.

Mukilteo did not actually see a stampede of developers looking to get involved with Lot 5, as first reported by the Puget Sound Business Journal , with the RFQ only producing one response. Kirkland-based MainStreet Property Group, which has built nearly 4,000 units across Seattle and the Eastside in recent years, expects to explore a multifamily mixed-use development with below-grade parking, the Journal reported late last month when the RFQ closed.

Though any actual redevelopment proposal remains theoretical at this point, this week the Mukilteo City Council did remove a major impediment that was standing in the way of the city's vision: rezoning Lot 5 from open space to waterfront mixed-use on a 6-1 vote. That vote simply opens the door to broader uses of the parcel, with a potential full conversion to park space still allowed under Mukilteo's zoning if the city decided to change course.

"All you're saying is we're going to rezone that property. Any of those future decisions about leasing the property, what the specific development would look like, those will all still be in the council's hands," Andy Galuska, Mukilteo's Planning and Community Development Director, told councilmembers Monday night. "At no point is the council going to lose control of that process through approval of this rezone. The City still owns the property."
But the rezone still faced considerable community opposition, with a sizable faction of Mukilteo residents wanting the city to commit to maintaining the area as a public park.

"Why can't we just look at open space and water and some green grass and a promenade shore? A walking path, a bike path. Why do we have to muck it up in Mukilteo every time and crap up this beautiful waterfront that we have?" Mukilteo resident Kate Forrester said at a public hearing on the rezone last month. "I want my grandchildren to play down on the beach. You can't have too many parks. That is the only thing that makes a city beautiful. Don't concrete it. Believe me, I came from California, and it's all paved over now."

One major point of contention down the road is likely to be any residential component to a redevelopment proposal. Including housing above amenities built at the ground level is one way that a project on the site could become financially viable, but exactly how many units that would be is sure to be hotly debated in Mukilteo.

Mukilteo has seen tepid housing growth over the last decade, despite ample demand, earning the city a callout as a laggard in a 2023 Urban Institute report by Yonah Freemark analyzing the region's housing deficit. Mukilteo's population has been essentially flat since the 2020 census, according to state estimates that last pegged the city at 21,610 residents.
If the city were to pursuing housing on Lot 5, the issue remains of a covenant tied to the property that restricts residential use altogether.

"There was a condition that residential uses not be located on Lot Five because of the contamination," Galuska said. "So, if any developer or the City in the future wants to develop residential uses there, that would have to be removed. The City Attorney's looked at that provision and thinks that it could be removed if we can prove that site has had some cleanup done on it... if we got that to a level of cleanup where residential is appropriate, that that condition could be could be removed."

The Mukilteo waterfront is a very constrained space, with just one bridge over the railroad tracks for all traffic to get in and out of the area – a bridge that the state highway department is set to replace in the coming years.

The area is fairly well-served by Community Transit buses, but the Sound Transit commuter rail station that provides service to Downtown Seattle is set to be retired in 2033 as Snohomish County's leaders focus on delivering light rail to Everett. Unlike in nearby Edmonds, the city has no Amtrak service, so the sunset of commuter rail would end all train service to that station.

All of which is to say that the topic of parking will be a major issue no matter what ultimately moved forward, but part of the vision for the overall waterfront revamp is creating structured garages under buildings that would allow the sea of stalls surrounding Lighthouse Park to be put to better use. That vision could potentially involve a shuttle bus that serves the waterfront from elsewhere in Mukilteo.
After hearing from members of the public, Councilmember Bob Champion was the sole vote against approving the rezone.

"I kind of think we're jumping the gun. So I can't support changing Lot 5 from open space to mixed use. I think there's plenty of opportunity down the road," Champion said. "I think I counted nine out of every 10 emails I received was, just leave it as open space."
But the majority of the council appears ready to at least open the door to some type of transformation at the city's front door.

"If we choose not to do this today, and we need to go for a rezone later, it's going to put us a year backwards, right? We need to be lockstep with the Port of Everett," Councilmember James Sterba said. "I'm going to keep going back to access to the water. I hear that all the time in all the emails and in the residents that approach me: there will be enhanced access to the water. The plan, as it shows, is every 250 feet off the promenade, there's a way to get to the water. Some of the drawings are spectacular. While while I walk that area myself, it it's not conducive to staying there and hanging out, and really enjoying it because because it's a gravel lot."

Mayor Marine, who has pledged that the city will be a "creative, flexible, and responsive partner" with any developer who is ultimately chosen to advance a plan for the site, framed Monday's vote as a major step.

"This has been a long time in coming," Marine said. "So much time has been spent, and all this really does is moves us to the next level to decide ultimately what we're going to do with that property. It may be a park or it may be development."

articles.title: Pop Loser: Ego Death at a Republican Party
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: Welcome back to Pop Loser! This week, Hayley Williams has a suggestion for “Nazi bitches,” Kelly Clarkson admitted to being “obsessed” with AI (sigh), Chrissie Hynde shared one of her hottest takes yet, and Justin Timberlake finally apologized for his beatboxing phase. Huge news: I have a new favorite Roxy Music song. Plus, keep reading if you want to see Neil Young “hoover” some pistachios.

This week in Strangerland, instrumental rock trio Bering Sea stopped by the office for another episode of Noise Complaint . Jullianne Bell and I unleashed the first installment of our Scarecrow Psychotronic Movie challenge picks , offering a fucked-up movie recommendation for every day of October (you’re welcome!). Stay tuned for week two, dropping Thursday.

Ego Death at a Republican Party. During her show in California on Saturday, Hayley Williams exclaimed “fuck ICE” and “free motherfucking Palestine” from the stage. Shortly after, a spokesperson from the Department of Homeland Security issued a statement to Fox News —because of course they did—stating: “We suggest Ms. Williams to [sic] thank them for their service, not belittle their sacrifice.”
Williams got the last word, posting a screenshot of the DHS statement on her Instagram stories alongside the response : “And may I suggest all Nazi bitches suck on my fat dick.”

Miss AI-dependent. Kelly Clarkson shared some disappointing thoughts about AI on Bowen Yang and Matt Rodgers’ Las Culturistas podcast last week during their recurring “I Don’t Think So Honey” segment, in which host and guest rant about something that makes their blood boil for one minute. Clarkson must have missed the memo on this one, as she launched into a declaration of appreciation, gushing, “I love AI. There are very amazing things with AI that I am obsessed with—and I’m very into it artistically, too.” She declared that her only issue with said technology is when “AI artists” compete on a chart with humans, suggesting they should have their own, separate charts.

Justin Timberlake apologizes for beatboxing, but “can’t promise” it won’t happen again. Timberlake has issued many apologies in recent years, including to the women he’s wronged ( Britney Spears and Janet Jackson ) and for his DWI that “ ruined the tour .” This week, Timberlake took to the comment section of an Instagram video by pop culture historian Hannah Young’s, in which she addressed Timberlake’s history of compulsive beatboxing. He commented, “I often look back on that time as well. I still haven’t come up with any answers. I don’t know how to apologize enough for whatever those ambitions were.” He continued, “I hope you can forgive me. Also, I can’t promise I won’t do it again. God help us all.”

To each one’s own. Chrissie Hynde is no stranger to hot takes, good and bad. articles.title: Slog AM: Former Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes Now Has a Bullshit Job, Trump Wants Iran to Nuke LA and San Diego, Autumn Is Here
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: Former Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes will now bring home the bacon by way of the private sector. He joined MissionRT, a company that “advises law-enforcement agencies on leadership, technology, and organizational change.” Why does all of this remind me of that book by the late anarchist and anthropologist David Graeber, Bullshit Jobs, A Theory ? In Graeber’s words: “Provisional Definition 2: a bullshit job is a form of employment that is so completely pointless, unnecessary, or pernicious that even the employee cannot justify its existence.”

Bruiser, the only elk on Whidbey Island has died. He was beloved by the community, who, according to the Seattle Times , fed him “apples, corn and potatoes” during the 14 years he spent on what must have appeared to him to be pretty much heaven. He didn’t have much to do but go this way and that, and never once attempted to leave the way he arrived on the island: by swimming. The lone elk, a local icon, was famous for his tangled antlers. Earth, receive an honoured guest , Bruiser the bull is laid to rest.

For the next few days, expect what you will experience today: morning mists or fogs, and sunny afternoons. Also, have you seen the trees around town? Autumn is finally here, and the leaves, red and gold, are soon to fall, or are falling, or have fallen. There are few things more beautiful than the sight of summer’s glorious death. In fact, I wish it lasted longer. Lasted until late November. I also wish people who don’t like walking on summer’s demise would use a rake instead of that loud gas guzzling machine. Expect a high of 66.

What’s Trump up to now? During some rally in Nebraska, he recommended that Iran nuke San Diego and Los Angeles . Of course, he has nothing to offer rural voters—who are feeling great pain at the pump and grocery store—but more and more of the same anti-urban and anti-diversity “ psychological wage .” The president, however, failed to mention San Francisco. Why? My guess is from Yahoo Finance : “Nvidia stock rises to new highs as market cap closes in on $6 trillion.” LA just makes movies, and San Diego only has military bases.

What a 21st-century mess this is. The sister of an Arizona road rage victim, Christopher Pelkey, who was shot to death by Gabriel Horcasitas, used an AI video of her brother to ask the judge to go easy on the defendant . In the words of AI Pelkey: “To Gabriel Horcasitas, the man who shot me: It is a shame we encountered each other that day in those circumstances… In another life, we probably could have been friends. I believe in forgiveness.” Though the AI Pelkey was “loved” by the judge, he still gave Horcasitas the maximum sentence. But the court was so bewildered by this novel use of AI, that it ultimately threw out the ruling and “[remanded] for resentencing.” Unlike the court in the film Rashomon , which is set in 12th-century Japan, modern US courts have yet to accept testimonies from ghosts (AI or otherwise).

Dr. Paul Allen (yes, there is more than one of them, and some are still alive), a professor of anesthesiology at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center suspects that “the botched execution of Christa Pike,” resulted from the executor’s failure to place the needle into a vein. As a consequence the poison only reached “peripheral tissues in the arm.” This apparently explained the “arm throbbing” witnessed by observers.

Now let me tell you something. If you’re going to execute me, you must use electricity or a gun or rope because I, too, have veins that are nearly impossible to find. (If you want my blood, you have to abandon the inside of the elbow and instead go for the wrist, which, for some reason I’ve never understood, is not ideal and even despised by nurses and technicians.) Well, Christa Pike regained consciousnes s yesterday. She is even talking to the living, but sustained “severe damage to her arms.” Her lawyer expects a “long recovery.” Well put. Let her recovery last for as long as she lives. In short, the death penalty must be abolished.

A quick thought. Though the future for Christa Pike is presently unclear (will they or will they not make a second attempt to kill her?), this nearly unprecedented situation has nevertheless entered a metaphysical zone. Meaning, Pike’s predicament is no longer just legal, but now also has a supernatural aspect. This matters because we live in a very superstitious society, and so many will see the failure to execute Pike as nothing less than a sign from the other side. The Old One is clearly saying something to us mere mortals. And do you want to be the one who dismisses a message from the Old One? He clearly said: Let Pike live goddamnit . And, amazingly, she is still here, still in the world. Now, who are you “to go against the wind?”

Let me tell you a great ghost story. It involves a black hole. The question is this: Where does a black hole’s gravity come from? The rough answer: From the ghost of a star. A star that’s no longer around. What happened? During the collapsing process of forming an event horizon, a black hole’s point of no return, time around the star became slower and slower, the greater and greater the collapse. Finally, the dying star’s gravity froze , stopped in time, and became a ghost of gravity because its fallen star no longer communicates with the universe we observe. End of story.

There is a whole movement of philosophical thought —indeed, the dominant movement since Kant—that is convinced that all things require a relation to exist, correlationism, because how can anything, even numbers, exist without an observer. Yet, we know there are places in time and space that exist without relationships or encounters. For example, once, before the explosion of the star whose dust is our sun and before us, there was simply nothing where I am now (in my home office on October 7, 2026), and, if the open universe theory is correct, or if the big crunch theory is correct, there will also be in the future nothing where I am at this moment.

What I find most fascinating about the mind is it can relate with things—a lonely piece of ice drifting through space five billion years ago; the terrific density of a neutron star that is a billion years away from now. And yet, the mind knows these things can never be seen or exist in any sensible way. A big part of our real is wholly impossible.

articles.title: Zahilay Proposes Advancing RapidRide R Funding to Spur Bus Upgrades
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: King County Executive Girmay Zahilay has proposed to advance a significant portion of the funding for Seattle's RapidRide R Line , in the hopes of achieving an "accelerated delivery timeline." The project will run between Downtown Seattle and Rainier Beach and replace the current Route 7. It is currently slated for a 2032 ribbon-cutting, which Zahilay has touted the possibility of moving up.
However, early designs for the R Line are seeing pushback, over changes that are seen as degrading an existing bus route that is already one of King County Metro's busiest.

Out of the R Line's total $91.2 million expected cost, $64.4 million would be advanced into the current 2026-2027 budget, if the County Council signs off on Zahilay's "omnibus" budget proposal as transmitted last month. That cash advance comes in the wake of a decision to not seek federal dollars for the R Line, something that reflects a bleak federal transit environment and also a hope that Metro would be nimbler without federal strings attached.

Metro is planning R Line upgrades in conjunction with major planned repaving work on Rainier Avenue being advanced by the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). An overhaul of the corridor from S Jackson Street to S Walden Street in Mount Baker, being paired with maintenance work on S Henderson Street in Rainier Beach, is expected to cost the city more than $100 million and provides an opportunity to include changes like new bus lanes, enhanced sidewalks, or separated bike facilities.

"Our goal in accelerating this funding is to build a strong partnership with SDOT and bolster our shared commitment to this project," Callie Craighead, Zahilay's press secretary, told The Urbanist . "King County Metro and the Seattle Department of Transportation are actively working to develop plans for shared investments along the RapidRide R alignment that minimize construction and roadway impacts, save costs, and support an accelerated delivery timeline. We heard from SDOT that they would like King County to make a stronger funding commitment to the project to avoid another situation where uncertain funding leads to delays or pauses in the project."
As a bus route that bisects Zahilay's former county council district, the new County Executive has turned the corridor upgrade into one of his administration's major transit priorities.

"I'm challenging Metro to do anything in our power to work with the City of Seattle to build a quality product as fast as possible," Zahilay said at a Metro open house for the project in August. "Every single weekday people are relying on this [route], so I wouldn't be advocating for a RapidRide R on a personal level if I didn't know that it was going to make the service better."

The Route 7 currently carries more than 11,000 daily riders on weekdays, making it the busiest route in Metro's network that never leaves the City of Seattle. With light rail running along MLK Way in parallel with the Route 7 for much of its route, the bus is often the choice for shorter local trips, or downtown trips for riders who aren't able to easily get to the faster train.

Officials hope the R Line will be significantly faster than Route 7, in part due to bus stop consolidation. But when early design concepts presented at open houses this summer showed that a significant number of existing bus stops were on the table to be eliminated with the conversion to the R Line, concerns mounted that current 7 riders would have longer walks to access transit than they do today, and people with disabilities might lose access altogether.

The maps that Metro recently presented resurfaced some of the same issues that plagued the project in its first iteration, before being officially put back on the shelf in 2021 due to financial constraints.

"A RapidRide would reduce the number of stops on the route, which would make it harder for people who currently rely on their local route," Urbanist contributor Ashley Archibald wrote that year , in a story that references many of the same issues that community members are bringing up now.

In the name of speeding up trips, Metro's initial concept would have consolidated 67 stops along the entire corridor into 45, counting both northbound and southbound trips. Along the northern segment of Rainier Avenue, for example, three northbound stops between Judkins Park Station and 12th Avenue would be converted into just one stop at S Dearborn Street. Heading south from Judkins Park, riders would have only one opportunity – at S Walker Street – to deboard before getting to Mount Baker Station.

Estimates produced by Metro in 2020 showed a travel time savings of 7.3 minutes to 11.7 minutes with the R Line during peak hours by 2040, but a big portion of those savings were expected to come from bus lanes that SDOT has actually implemented along some segments of Rainier Avenue since that time. Metro has not yet released any updated time savings data for its current concepts that reflect the gains that have already been made in reliability for the 7.

"There's a lot of folks using the bus to travel locally within Rainier Valley, and commuting to downtown as efficiently as possible is not necessarily the top priority for a lot of folks who are using transit right now on this road," Anna Zivarts, founder and executive director of the Nondrivers Alliance, told The Urbanist .

This past weekend, Zivarts hosted a Route 7 ride with local mobility advocates and elected officials to present them with an up-close view of who is actually using the bus today. In attendance were State Senator Rebecca Saldaña and Port Commissioner Toshiko Hasegawa – both are campaigning to become the next King County Councilmember for District 2 – as well as Seattle Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck and 37th Legislative District state house candidate Kelabe Tewolde. The event was timed with the annual Week Without Driving .

Rinck noted that Rainier Avenue was included in her "Better Bus Lanes" budget proposal that was unanimously approved last year, along with the successful Denny Way bus lanes that were installed this summer .

"We've made progress on bus lanes. We now need the frequency to match the need, and so that is why I'm really excited about RapidRide R, particularly from the frequency components that will come with it," Rinck told The Urbanist following the ridealong. "I have some outstanding concerns about the stop elimination plan, and I'm curious to learn more about what the county is thinking on that front. But the city is going to need to be a partner in those infrastructure improvements to support that project coming online. I'm really committed to working with riders and future riders of the 7/RapidRide R to make sure that it's meeting community needs."

Metro spokesperson Al Sanders told The Urbanist that the agency is still actively developing an updated proposal for RapidRide R, ahead of a potential King County Council vote confirming the route's alignment and planned stop locations next month.

"Rescoping work for the R Line is still underway," Sanders said. "Metro is using what we’ve been hearing from the community, along with updated technical analysis, to help identify the highest-priority elements of the project. Because the corridor and travel patterns have changed since the original concept was developed, this step is critical to making sure the final design reflects current needs."

While the proposals presented this summer weren't much changed from the previous iteration of the R Line, the refreshed plans may be more aligned with current needs along the corridor and more responsive to critiques from riders.

"While we are still compiling all of the input, we have heard strong support for increased investment in transportation infrastructure in South Seattle and that riders want fast, reliable transit service throughout the Rainier Valley. We are also hearing that stop locations and walking distance are important to Route 7 riders," Sanders continued.
Craighead said that Zahilay's office has been engaged with Metro when it comes to what that updated proposal looks like.

"Our team is actively working with King County Metro to develop a RapidRide R alignment proposal to transmit to the King County Council," Craighead told The Urbanist . "Executive Zahilay and members of his staff joined open houses about the project this summer to hear community feedback directly and are working with Metro to incorporate that feedback into the proposal. Delivering long-promised and long-overdue transit investments to South Seattle continues to be a priority for the Executive."

It will ultimately fall on Zahilay's office and the Metro team to thread the needle on what is already an intensely beloved bus, even if frequent bus bunching and overcrowding does get on riders' nerves.

"If we're trying to entice people into riding transit who have other options already, that's a different priority than meeting the needs of people who are already relying on transit and don't have other options in the Rainier Valley, and that's a very large population here," Zivarts said. "And so I worry with this RapidRide proposal, it's focused more on the theoretical person who might be enticed to ride transit if their commute was shorter, versus the people who need it to get to the grocery store, the pharmacy, or whatever they need to do along this corridor."

articles.title: Duplicative services and commuter route truncation, again
articles.author: Sherwin Lee
paras: We’re about a month into the Fall shakeup, where a substantial number of service changes were implemented to improve connections to Link. This is a recurring playbook that Metro has used ever since light rail service began: identify duplicative services and restructure existing bus routes to connect to Link stations rather than running all the way into downtown Seattle.

When Northgate Link opened, Sound Transit truncated many of its 510 series routes to connect at Link instead. After Lynnwood Link, all of Community Transit’s direct services to downtown Seattle were restructured . And with the August changes , both Metro and Sound Transit no longer offer any one-seat rides from Bellevue or Issaquah to Seattle, save for the 2 Line.

Critics of this approach generally lament the loss of the one-seat ride, that trip times generally increase when factoring in wait times, and that Link is not necessarily faster point-to-point than express routes. The Sound Transit subreddit and other various community forums feature countless examples of riders testifying to that end. There is even now a “Restore 554” petition circulating among Issaquah residents, urging the restoration of a direct Issaquah-Seattle route.

The planning justifications for this type of restructuring are quite straightforward: Link provides a frequent high-capacity serve to major regional centers; instead of running costly peak-directional bus service, reinvest the hours into boosting local connecting service. This implementation aligns with Jarrett Walker’s “frequency is freedom” mantra and is generally a position this blog has supported.

In practice, however, real-world conditions can muddy the picture. Take, for example, the 554’s successor: the 556, which now provides frequent all-day service between Issaquah and Bellevue. Those previously using the 554 (or the 550 local stops along Bellevue Way) to get to Seattle must now connect at South Bellevue Station for the same trip.

These transfer conditions can greatly deteriorate due to local northbound congestion on Bellevue Way just in the short span between the I-90 off-ramp and the station bus stops. Riders agonizingly wait for traffic to crawl up Bellevue Way only to see Seattle-bound trains glide past over their heads. Even in the southbound direction, buses have to yield to northbound traffic in order to turn into the station bays, which adds travel time variability.
The physical infrastructure in between the connecting services is important too. Jarrett Walker touches on this point in one of his foundational articles on transferring:

… the unpleasantness of the connection experience depends on many details of how the connection works. If two buses or trains arrive on opposite sides of a platform, facing one another five meters apart, with their doors open at the same time, walking out of one and into the other is a pretty low level of inconvenience for most passengers. If the connection involves getting off a bus, crossing a busy street, and waiting for another bus not knowing when it will arrive, the inconvenience is much greater.

As it were, the connecting infrastructure at South Bellevue and Mercer Island stations is less than ideal. Both settings require a moderate walk (across a signalized intersection in the latter case, largely thanks to Mercer Island’s opposition to an 80th Ave transfer point) and ascending or descending to the train platform. This can add a lot of variability, particularly for those with limited mobility, on top of the wait for the connecting service.

Negative feedback is often amplified over positive feedback, as human beings are far more likely to complain about things that hurt them rather than praise the things that help them. But in many ways, what is often seen as a degradation in one part of the network typically means an improvement in another part.

554 riders, for example, might glowingly reminisce about the quick travel times across I-90, but forget about the frequent outbound reliability issues inflicted by 2nd Avenue congestion (as I so often personally experienced). And although not quite a zero sum game, the changes have meant a substantially better commute for Issaquah-Bellevue riders, among other parts of the system.

Big restructures in the regional network will invariably result in system-wide tradeoffs, but that doesn’t mean agencies’ hands are tied. Barring a miraculous way of sending buses congestion-free right up (or down) to the Link platforms, transfer penalties can be offset by improving frequency and reliability across all segments.

Making the 556 a frequent all-day route that connects to frequent 2 Line service is certainly an excellent start, but continued work on reliability improvements are always in order. This might mean more attentive maintenance to ensure fewer breakdowns of Link trains. Or it could mean stronger partnerships with WSDOT and local jurisdictions to give signal or lane priority to buses.

Whatever the solution, transit agencies cannot go it alone here. Route 8’s dramatic reliability leaps were only possible by some repainting (and other minor infrastructural improvements) from SDOT. In the same way, local jurisdictions owe it to the taxpaying public to squeeze out the full return on our massive regional investment in transit. Helping create reliable well-connected services is a small, but important step to get there.
